entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing
entry.content:
In the previous chapters, we went through the setup of the V2G-device configurations and the installation of those devices, ultimately allowing us to enter MR results in both kWh for charging and discharging and MIN for the availability bonus.

This chapter will be dedicated to the billing and invoicing aspect of the V2G-installations. As established in the previous chapter, three register-permissible rates were created with the sole purpose of registering the consumptions:

  • CO_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of charging quantity in kWh
  • COMP_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of discharging quantity in kWh
  • TIME_V2G_E – Registering of connection time in MIN and conversion to HRS

Billing schema E_V2G_SCH

Once the register-permissible rates have registered and transferred the quantities, a facts-permissible rate is required to calculate the amounts based on the measured quantities.

In the context of this V2G set-up, a new rate “E_V2G_BILL” was created. All rate steps calculating an amount simply use the QUANTI01 variant which allows for a quantity to be multiplied by a quantity-based price to calculate an amount.

IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL – rate steps

The following IS-U prices were configured in our SAP S/4HANA system and stored in the operands with type QPRICE at rate facts level:

  • E_V2G_C+ – Price for charging at 0,3297 EUR/kWh

  • E_V2G_C- – Price for discharging at -0,40 EUR/kWh

  • E_V2G_TCON – Price for availability bonus at -0,24/HR

Unlike the quantity-based prices used to calculate an amount based on the consumptions registered in kWh, price “E_V2G_TCON” must be configured with a UoM in HRS:

IS-U quantity-based price E_V2GTCON with UoM “hrs”

As established in the previous chapter (V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 2): From Meter Reading Results to Billable Quantities), the quantities originally registered in MIN will already have been converted by rate “TIME_V2G_E”. This allows us to directly apply a price per hour for the availability bonus.

Finally, to store the quantity-based price with a UoM of HRS, the QPRICE operand in which the price will be stored must have a matching UoM:

QPRICE Operand E_V2G_TPR

Overview of the rate facts in E_V2G_BILL:

IS-U Rate E_V2G_BILL – Rate facts within fact group V2G

After configuring the facts-permissible rate that calculates the amounts, a facts-permissible rate type will be required to create the rate determination. For these examples, rate type “E_V2G_EBIL” was created and stored in a RATETYPE operand in the installation facts of both installations for each respective scenario.

Rate determination for IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL

Installation 4100000512:

Installation 4100000512 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts

Installation 4100000513:

Installation 4100000513 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts

The IS-U billing and invoicing runs can now be executed for both installations, regardless of the respective device configuration. When analysing the billing documents, we can now filter for the posting-relevant lines. These lines show the amounts calculated by multiplying the quantities registered in kWh by the corresponding quantity-based prices and, more importantly, the amount calculated based on the number of hours the vehicle has been connected to the grid for the availability bonus.

Scenario 1 – Billing document 100000005504

Scenario 2 – Billing document 100000005503

While we are still looking at the billing process, I would also like to highlight another interesting aspect of the availability bonus, namely the fact that the reimbursed connection time could be limited. As a possible commercial rule, the reimbursed connection time could be limited to 250 hours per month. With the hourly price used in this example, the availability bonus would therefore be capped at EUR 60 per month. This is also something I integrated in the E_V2G_BILL rate by adding the IF01 variant which allows us to compare the values of two quantity operands:

In this example, we compare the hourly quantity stored in operand E_V2G_CHR to the quantity stored in operand E_V2G_T250. The latter is fixed at 250 hours in the rate category facts:

Rate category facts of E_V2G_RC : fixed quantity of 250 hours

If the number of hours registered for the availability bonus exceeds the limit of 250 hours, the amount is calculated based on the fixed quantity of 250 hours stored in E_V2G_T250 (rate step 5). Otherwise, the amount is calculated based on the originally measured number of hours stored in E_V2G_CHR (rate step 7). To illustrate this, if the meter reading result were 18.000 MIN, it would be converted to 300 HRS. In that case, the availability bonus would therefore be calculated based on 250 hours, while the remaining 50 hours would not be included in the calculation.

The example below illustrates what this could look like on a billing document:

Billing document 100000005502 – measured quantity of 18.000 MIN exceeding the 250-hour limit.

Before we move on to the results of the invoicing run for both scenarios, I would like to point out that for these examples I do not intend to apply any taxes for the availability bonus. On top of that, I also wanted to ensure that the lines for the availability bonus would be displayed on a separate line on the print document.

For that reason, I created dedicated FI-CA sub-transactions for the availability bonus:

Table TE305 – Sub-transactions for availability bonus: 0250 (Debit) – 0251 (Credit)

Using dedicated sub-transactions allows the availability bonus to be distinguished from the energy-related charges within the FI-CA and invoicing processes. And of course, these sub-transactions are configured on the lines that calculate the amount for the availability bonus in the E_V2G_BILL rate:

IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL - sub-transactions for availability bonus configured in the rate steps

In addition, a separate tax determination, “V0”, linked to tax code “V0” with a 0% tax rate was configured for the availability bonus. This was done to ensure that the availability bonus remains distinguishable from the discharging remuneration during invoicing and is displayed as a separate line on the print document:

Chart of Accounts 2500 – Account assignment for availability bonus

Tax code V0 – 0% tax rate

For the purpose of this blog, the availability bonus is modelled as a separate remuneration for the availability service rather than as a discount that is simply deducted from the energy charge. The actual tax and accounting treatment would depend on the applicable commercial and regulatory framework and is outside the scope of this blog.

Now we can finally execute the invoicing run and review the results:

Scenario 1 – Print document 2000000226

Scenario 2 – Print document 2000000227

As illustrated by the examples above, the availability bonus is displayed as a separate line on the print document, without any tax amount being calculated.

 

With the billing rate, quantity-based prices and corresponding rate determination configured, the two V2G scenarios can now be billed using the quantities registered by the devices.

The examples demonstrate that standard SAP IS-U billing functionality can be used to calculate amounts for both energy quantities measured in kWh and connection time originally recorded in minutes and converted to hours. The same billing logic can be applied to both device setups, regardless of whether the kWh and MIN quantities are registered by a single device or by separate devices.

Most importantly, both the billing documents and print documents confirm the flow from the original meter reading results through quantity processing and unit conversion to the final calculated amounts. This demonstrates how standard IS-U configuration can be used to model and bill selected commercial aspects of a Vehicle-to-Grid scenario without requiring custom billing and invoicing logic.

In the next chapter, we will explore an alternative solution. Rather than managing the entire V2G meter-to-cash flow in IS-U, we will investigate how Convergent Invoicing can be used to calculate the availability bonus and integrate it with IS-U without having to maintain the MR results recorded in MIN.

entry.title: Exploring AI and key innovations in SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS2
entry.content:
SAP is building the Autonomous Enterprise — an operating model where AI is not a separate tool but a force embedded directly into the operational core, executing work end to end. The SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS2 (also referred to as SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2) release accelerates this shift, expanding agentic AI across finance, supply chain, asset management, sales, service, and product design.

At the top sits Joule — the new engagement layer where people, data, workflows, and agents come together across SAP systems and beyond. Underneath, the SAP Autonomous Suite reimagines how enterprises run through three coordinated layers:

  • Joule Assistants are role-aligned AI teammates — each designed around a specific business function such as financial closing, cash management, or logistics. They understand your context and coordinate the right agents to deliver the outcome you need.
  • Joule Agents are the specialized doers. Each agent handles a specific multi-step task — calculating accruals, screening maintenance requests, resolving invoice discrepancies — reasoning over live business data and acting autonomously within defined guardrails.
  • Embedded AI features power everyday Fiori applications with natural-language search, smart summarization, AI-assisted filtering, and error explanation — intelligence built directly into the screen, no agent orchestration required.

Industry AI adds vertical depth — process knowledge, compliance rules, and data models specific to your industry, embedded from day one. And the SAP Business AI Platform provides the foundation everything runs on: unified data, business context, and enterprise-grade governance.

 

*Disclaimer: The Joule Assistants and Agents described in this post are currently available through SAP's Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. General availability is planned to begin in Q4 2026, with rollout continuing into Q1 2027. Not all agents require SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2 — minimum system requirements vary by agent, and support for additional releases is being continuously extended through downports. For the latest on which releases support which agents, refer to SAP Note 3789370, which is updated on an ongoing basis, and the SAP Discovery Center. All other AI innovations covered in this post (embedded AI features, Joule skills, and machine learning scenarios) are generally available with the 2025 FPS2 release unless noted otherwise. This blog is a living document and will be updated as new assistants and agents become available in the coming weeks and months. The information here reflects publicly available SAP product documentation and roadmap materials as of October 2026. All forward-looking statements are subject to change.

 

With this release, SAP significantly expands both the number of assistants and the depth of agent coverage across the suite. Here is what is new.

Part A: Joule Assistants and Agents

 

Finance: Autonomous Intelligence Across the Financial Lifecycle

Finance is the largest area of AI investment in FPS2, with new agents and assistants organized across the Autonomous Finance portfolio — from accounting and close, to treasury, revenue management, and compliance.

Financial Closing Assistant

 

The Financial Closing Assistant orchestrates the agents managing the period close, with users controlling each agent's level of engagement for handling journal postings, clearing activities, and analysis. Its tasks include: clearing receivables and payables; calculating and posting accounting accruals; posting journal entries; resolving errors and detecting anomalies in asset accounting; analyzing financial consistency and surfacing bottlenecks; reconciling goods receipt/invoice receipt and intercompany transactions (including matching unstructured intercompany invoices); managing fixed-asset master data and reviewing general ledger accounts; and clearing general ledger balances with final review, KPI analysis, and executive-summary generation. assistant is coordinated by the Financial Closing Orchestration Agent and includes the Journal Entry Agent for recommending and posting general-ledger entries with an evidence trail, the Accounting Accruals Agent for analyzing historical data and preparing accrual journal entries, the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent, the Financial Consistency Analysis Agent for identifying hidden process inconsistencies and the Asset Accounting Anomaly Detection Agent for flagging potentially inaccurate postings. (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

 

Accounts Receivable Assistant

 

The Accounts Receivable Assistant helps finance teams accelerate cash collection, resolve disputes efficiently, and manage credit risk proactively, providing a 360-degree customer view that surfaces overdue items, balances, dispute cases, promises to pay, resubmissions, and contact history. Its capabilities span collection worklist management, dispute management, and dunning insights — focusing collectors on critical accounts, surfacing next-best-action recommendations, preparing customer communications, creating and resolving disputes from emails or Joule prompts, and analyzing payment history with AI-based matching and aging-pattern analysis. The assistant coordinates specialized agents: the Accounts Receivable Orchestration Agent, the Collection Account Preparation Agent for delivering instant account insights and preparing collection calls, the Dispute Creation Agent for creating dispute cases and validating documents and duplicates, the Dispute Resolution Agent for providing context and recommending resolution actions, the Dunning Insights Agent for analyzing payment history and providing AR recommendations and the Receivable Account Analysis Agent for visibility into balances, invoices, aging, disputes, and dunning levels.(SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

 

Accounts Payable Assistant

 

The Accounts Payable Assistant transforms AP with AI-powered automation — eliminating manual payments, automating bank validations, and resolving exceptions instantly while predicting payment risks, detecting clearing patterns, and surfacing real-time insights on DPO, aging, and cash flow. Its capabilities span six areas: payment inquiry, which captures requests, triggers payments, and sends status updates; pre-validation, which validates attributes, checks compliance, performs risk checks, and recommends fixes; bank validation, which verifies supplier bank accounts, automates risk checks, and recommends corrective actions; exceptions, which flags, explains, and routes payment exceptions; vendor analytics, which tracks DPO, cash flow, and discount opportunities and identifies operational improvements; and reconciliation, which reconciles statements and highlights discrepancies. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Accounts Payable Orchestration Agent and the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent for AI-based matching and aging-pattern analysis to generate clearing recommendations. (SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

Recurring Receivables Assistant

 

The Recurring Receivables Assistant helps finance teams automate and optimize the order-to-cash process for recurring billing and subscription-based business models, deploying finance agents that accelerate cash collection, resolve disputes, and identify and act on revenue at risk. Its capabilities span convergent invoicing, subscription contract changes, invoice correction orchestration, collections prioritization, dispute resolution, 360-degree customer account visibility, and payment matching with continuously improving matching rules. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Subscription Lifecycle Agent for managing subscription contract changes with compliant updates, the Convergent Invoice Execution Agent for detecting invoice issues and executing compliant fixes and the Collection Insights Agent for recommending next-best actions prioritized by cash impact and customer insights.(SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

Sales: Agentic Order Fulfillment and Expanded Conversational Capabilities

Sales Operations Assistant

 

The Sales Operations Assistant enables sales teams to quickly identify fulfillment issues, receive recommended resolutions, and create or update sales documents directly in their workflow — minimizing manual rework and delays, reducing order-to-cash cycle time, and improving customer satisfaction. Its capabilities span two core areas: order entry, which supports uploading unstructured purchase-order files, extracting and validating data, reviewing order requests, and converting them into sales orders; and order monitoring and issue resolution, which covers supply, credit, billing, and delivery issues — including recommending corrective actions, removing blocks, and creating or updating sales documents after human approval. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Billing Block Resolution Agent, the Credit Block Issues Resolution Agent, the Delivery Issue Resolution Agent, and the Supply Issue Resolution Agent (SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

 

Supply Chain, Manufacturing, and Logistics

The supply chain and manufacturing areas receive targeted AI enhancements in FPS2, with a focus on production planning intelligence, quality management automation, and warehouse operations support.

Logistics Assistant

 

The Logistics Assistant brings AI-driven coordination to warehouse operations, helping keep day-to-day logistics running efficiently. In this release for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, it focuses on two critical areas: batch lifecycle management and warehouse resource optimization. On the batch side, the assistant continuously monitors batch expiration across inventory and triggers actions to minimize waste — ensuring perishable or time-sensitive goods are consumed or moved before they expire. On the warehouse floor, it facilitates optimal resource allocation by analyzing workload patterns and proactively flagging potential resource shortages before they impact operations. The assistant coordinates with two specialized agents: the Batch Optimization Agent, which autonomously tracks expiry timelines and initiates corrective actions, and the Warehouse Workload Optimization Agent, which balances labor and capacity to keep throughput on target (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

 

Asset Management: A New Level of Intelligence for Maintenance and Operations

Asset management receives the most comprehensive agent expansion in this release, with a suite of new Joule Agents — orchestrated by the Asset Operations Assistant — designed to support the entire maintenance lifecycle from equipment onboarding to job debriefing.

 

Asset Operations Assistant

 

The Asset Operations Assistant orchestrates AI agents across reliability, maintenance planning, scheduling, and execution to turn asset signals into coordinated maintenance action and improve uptime. It interprets equipment signals and requests to prioritize work, aligns resources and readiness, and uses execution outcomes to continuously improve asset performance. Its tasks include: assessing asset alerts and recommending next-best actions; creating and prioritizing maintenance work based on asset conditions, business priorities, and operational needs; optimizing maintenance schedules and workforce assignments; and briefing technicians and summarizing completed work. The assistant coordinates six specialized agents: the Equipment Insights Agent for complete equipment insights supporting better decisions, planning, and reliability; the Maintenance Event Planning Agent for avoiding disruptions with real-time insights, smart updates, and planning support; the Maintenance Job Debrief Agent for streamlining maintenance job debriefs with AI-driven recommendations and insights; the Maintenance Request Initiation Agent for instantly creating and routing maintenance requests from natural language inputs; the Maintenance Task List Management Agent for automating task list creation, boosting consistency, and reducing effort; and the Operational Maintenance Planning Agent for avoiding disruptions with real-time insights, smart updates, and planning support (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

R&D / Engineering

 

Product Design Assistant

 

The Product Design Assistant is an AI-driven system of agents that connects data across product development and downstream processes. It analyzes product information, supports change decisions, ensures compliance, and coordinates collaboration — helping teams move faster, reduce rework, and deliver higher-quality products. Its tasks include: analyzing product designs, recipes, and specifications; preparing product changes including scoping and assessing impacts; validating compliance and requirements across product and recipe data; extracting, classifying, and improving product data quality; setting up collaborations, tracking tasks, and creating notifications; and preparing product data for handover to production and supply chain execution. The assistant coordinates two specialized agents: the Change Record Management Agent for reducing cost and accelerating time-to-market and the Product Data Maintenance Agent for assisting design engineers who work with product master data in SAP S/4HANA (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

Procurement

 

Receiving Assistant

The Receiving Assistant is a new Joule Assistant for procurement that simplifies goods receipt, service entry sheet processing, and returns by automating tasks, streamlining workflows, and guiding users through complex receiving scenarios. In this release, the assistant introduces the Return Goods to Supplier Agent — a specialized agent that detects goods with slow or no movement in inventory and optimizes and automates the returns process back to the supplier. Instead of requiring procurement or warehouse teams to manually identify stagnant stock, investigate root causes, and initiate return purchase orders, the agent continuously monitors inventory movement patterns and triggers the returns workflow autonomously. This reduces the manual effort involved in identifying returnable goods, accelerates the returns cycle, and helps organizations recover value from unused or slow-moving inventory. The result: lower carrying costs, improved working capital, and a cleaner inventory position — all driven by machine learning rather than periodic manual reviews (SAP | Learn more).

 

Part B: Embedded AI Innovations

 

AI-assisted enterprise search in the SAP Fiori launchpad to search for form bundles and contract objects

 

AI-assisted enterprise search in the SAP Fiori launchpad extends natural-language search to form bundles and contract objects, allowing users to type plain-language queries in the launchpad search bar and retrieve relevant results without navigating complex filter structures. The feature targets a larger and more specific result set from less-specific queries, reducing the time users spend locating the right form bundle or contract object. It builds on the broader AI-assisted enterprise search capability already available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition for objects such as sales orders, billing documents, and purchase orders — and is listed as a future release for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (SAP Discovery Center).

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Service Contracts

This feature extends natural language search in the SAP Fiori launchpad to service contracts, enabling users to find contracts using plain language queries with instant responses. It eliminates the need to learn system syntax or complex filters, simplifying adoption and reducing training needs while delivering results in a single search interaction.

 

AI-Assisted Defect Creation (Quality Management)

Joule now enables quality engineers and technicians to create defect records through natural language — including from uploaded source documents such as invoices, delivery notes, or photographs of a defective part. Instead of manually navigating screens and populating fields, users simply describe the issue or attach a document, and Joule extracts the key data — material number, batch, quantity, reference documents, customer or supplier information, defect description, and defect code — then calls the Defects API to create a pre-filled record. The capability supports Generic Defects, Production Defects, and Warehouse Defects (types 06, 07, and 08). Once created, users review and complete the defect in the Manage Defects app. Under the hood, the feature runs on the QM_DEFECT_DOCSUMMARY intelligent scenario and requires activation through Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM). Available from 2025 FPS02 (SAP Help).

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Bill of Distribution (BOD) 

Enables natural language search for bill of distribution data, simplifying navigation and accelerating access to critical logistics information for planning and distribution teams.

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Batches in the SAP Fiori Launchpad

This feature extends natural language search to batches within the SAP Fiori launchpad, displaying key data including shelf-life expiration date, manufacturing date, batch status, country of origin, supplier, material, and plant. It enhances the search experience by allowing users to find batch data using everyday language.

 

AI-Generated Business Insights in Cost Center Review Booklet (Finance)

 AI-generated summaries now enhance the cost center review booklet, providing deeper financial oversight by analyzing and validating both actual and planned cost data. Business users get faster, more informed analysis with insights that would previously have required manual review of multiple reports.

 

 

Performance and Flexibility for Behavioral Insights (Collections Management for Contract Accounting)

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition includes an AI-supported capability called Behavioral Insights for Contract Accounting — a machine learning solution that analyzes historical customer data to predict and explain payment risk. Collection specialists use these risk scores and insights to quickly identify high-risk accounts, optimize collection strategies, and reduce outstanding debts and write-offs. Results integrate directly into existing dunning and collections workflows.

The 2025 FPS2 release strengthens this capability across three dimensions. First, performance enhancements now support significantly larger datasets within the models, enabling organizations with high-volume receivables to run predictions at scale. Second, flexibility enhancements introduce support for multiple contract account categories within a single solution — a change that directly enables public sector organizations managing multiple tax types to leverage behavioral insights across their full portfolio. Third, a new ability to accommodate test datasets where the data may not be current makes it easier and faster to validate and deploy machine learning scenarios in non-production environments.

A key architectural advantage remains: the solution keeps data in place within SAP S/4HANA, eliminating the need for data extraction or replication. This reduces deployment risk, accelerates time to value, and ensures that sensitive customer data never leaves the system boundary.

 

 

Create Sales Orders from Unstructured Data with Document AI (Sales)

Internal sales representatives can now create sales orders directly from purchase order files in PDF, email, or image formats. The system leverages premium Document AI (AnyDox) to automatically extract file information and propose values for sales order fields — with multi-language support and instant learning capabilities. This significantly reduces manual data entry and accelerates order processing, especially in high-volume environments.

 

AI-Assisted Management of Expiring Service Contracts with Joule Skill (Service)

This feature enables users to search for expiring service contract items within a user-defined time frame via Joule and run extension scenarios including configuring auto-renewal, renewing and creating new service contracts, renewing entire contracts or specific line items, and providing quick actions for expiring contracts. It allows service teams to manage contract tasks through natural language requests, providing fast navigation and targeted guidance for renewing or extending contracts.

 

Joule-Based Search and Status Update of Service Contracts with Joule Skill (Service)

Users can now search for service contracts or contract items by employee and product name directly in Joule, and change lifecycle status to "released" or "complete" within the same conversational experience. This combines search and updates in a single interaction, reducing clicks and context switching while minimizing administrative overhead for contract managers.

 

 

AI-Assisted Processing of Incoming Quality Certificates

This capability, cross-ported from SAP Cloud ERP, automates the extraction and validation of data from supplier quality certificates. It delivers immediate efficiency gains by reducing manual effort in quality management — a high-usage area where even small improvements have a significant impact. In parallel, Joule for App Navigation in Quality Management now enables users to instantly navigate to more than 15 core QM Fiori apps using natural language queries.

 

Master Data Management

 

Joule for Data Provider Integration in Business Partner Governance

This feature enables users to search for business partner reference records from external data providers directly within Joule, display details including name, address, and identification numbers, and create a business partner from a selected reference record with pre-populated fields. It simplifies data governance through a conversational interface, improves data quality, and reduces manual entry by transferring reference data directly into the creation flow.

 

Joule for Business Partners — Central Governance

Users can now ask Joule in natural language to search, display, and edit business partner data, including address, communication, bank, and identification data. This delivers a consumer-grade experience for master data processing, increasing effectiveness, speed, and automation in business partner governance. Available in cloud-ready mode in SAP Master Data Governance.

 

 

AI-Assisted Validation Rule Creation in Joule

Joule can now create validation rules using AI, automatically deriving values such as the base table from a provided description. It also checks for duplicates to determine if a similar rule already exists in the system — increasing efficiency, reducing manual effort, and maintaining system integrity.

 

User-Experience

 

AI-Assisted Filtering Using Natural Language for SAP Fiori Elements Apps

Users can now filter list report applications built with SAP Fiori elements using conversational terms alongside system-defined filters. The feature supports query reuse, including saving favorite queries and accessing last-used ones — making data access more intuitive across all Fiori elements-based applications.

entry.title: JV Cycles or Standard CO Cycles? What Really Changes When You Allocate Costs in SAP JVA, Part-1
entry.content:
In a JVA environment, month-end allocations aren't only a controlling exercise. Every euro that moves from a shared cost center to a venture ends up on a partner's billing statement, or deliberately doesn't. That's why it's worth understanding exactly what separates the JV-specific cycles from the standard CO cycles.

Two families of cycles

Standard cost center allocations use assessment (KSU1/KSU5) and distribution (KSV1/KSV5). SAP Joint Venture Accounting provides its own equivalents: JV assessment (GJF1/GJF5) and JV distribution (GJG1/GJG5).

 

 To see what actually differs, I created a standard distribution cycle (KSV1) and a JV distribution cycle (GJG1) side by side in an SAP S/4HANA sandbox.

What's the same

Almost everything:

  • Header screens are identical: the same indicators (Iterative, Cumulative, Derive Functional Area) and the same field groups.
  • Segment Header tabs are identical: the same sender rules, share percentage, receiver rules and tracing factor options.
  • Neither needs an allocation cost element, because both are distributions and keep the original cost elements.

In other words, the JV cycle isn't a separate allocation tool. It uses the same CO allocation logic.

 

One note if you repeat this comparison: compare assessment with assessment (KSU1 vs GJF1) and distribution with distribution (KSV1 vs GJG1). An assessment has fields a distribution doesn't need, such as the assessment cost element, and those differences have nothing to do with JVA.

What's different: the recovery indicator layer

Two things appear in GJG1 that don't exist in KSV1:

  1. A JV recovery indicator field in the segment.
  2. An Account Assignment tab, where manipulation rules can be maintained at a more detailed level than the segment.

Both exist for one reason. The recovery indicator on each allocated line decides whether that cost is billable to partners, and a JV cycle has to determine it.

This isn't optional. If a JV cycle can't find a manipulation rule, either in the segment or in the account assignment, it can't determine a recovery indicator and stops with an error (message G4804). A standard KSV/KSU cycle has no such check. It moves the cost and leaves the recovery indicator to the system's normal determination.

Where the rules live: GJCS

The manipulation rules themselves are maintained per controlling area in GJCS. The structure has two levels:

  • Manipulation rule: the rule key and description. You reference this key in the JV cycle.
  • Recovery indicator relations: the mapping. For a given sender recovery indicator (and cost element), it defines which recovery indicator the resulting lines receive.

 

A practical tip: in a new system or sandbox, GJCS may be completely empty. In that case, every JV cycle will fail until at least one rule and its relations are defined. Build and test the rules before you build the cycles.

A hypothetical field scenario

This example is hypothetical. An operator runs a shared logistics cost center supporting two operated ventures. The costs are distributed by a statistical key figure (SKF), such as crew days. Under the joint operating agreement, most of these costs are billable, but a corporate portion isn't.

The consultant defines a manipulation rule in GJCS. Billable sender costs stay billable on the receiver side, and non-billable costs stay non-billable. The rule is assigned in a GJG1 cycle, with the venture cost objects as receivers.

Before running, validate that:

  • the receivers carry the correct venture and equity group data;
  • the manipulation rule covers every sender cost element and recovery indicator combination the sender can carry;
  • a test run in GJG5 completes without recovery indicator errors.

After the run, reconcile:

  • the sender credit against the receiver debits;
  • billable and non-billable totals per venture;
  • everything before cutback runs, so corrections don't have to be reversed after billing.

When KSV/KSU still makes sense

Standard cycles remain the right choice for allocations between objects with no venture relevance, such as head-office cost centers that never reach partner billing. Tooling can also differ by release, so check what applies to your system before standardizing.

Checklist before choosing or running a cycle

  1. Are any senders or receivers venture-relevant?
  2. Is the manipulation rule defined in GJCS, with complete recovery indicator relations?
  3. Is the rule assigned in the cycle segment or its Account Assignment tab?
  4. Does the cycle run before cutback in the period-end sequence?
  5. Has a test run been reconciled per venture and per recovery indicator?

Takeaway

On the surface, a JV cycle and a standard cycle look almost identical. The difference is one layer deep, but it's the layer partners care about. A JV cycle won't post an allocation until it knows whether the cost is billable. If an allocation affects what partners pay, that's exactly the control you want.

In Part 2, I'll walk through the JV recovery indicator field, the Account Assignment tab and a working manipulation rule in detail.

How does your organization split JV and standard CO allocations? I'd be glad to hear from other JVA consultants/practitioners in the comments.

Further reading

  • SAP Help Portal – Introduction to Joint Venture Accounting (JVA)
  • SAP Community – Month End Closing Allocations for Upstream Companies

entry.title: SD Credit Management: 5-Level Approval Workflow for Credit-Blocked Sales Orders
entry.content:
In SAP Sales and Distribution, credit management helps control customer exposure by checking the customer's credit limit when a Sales Order is created.

In a customer implementation, I worked on a requirement where a Sales Order should still be saved when the credit limit is exceeded, but it should be credit blocked for delivery until the required business approval is completed. To address this, we implemented a 5-level workflow-based Credit Management approval process.

Business Requirement

Sales Order → Credit Check → Credit Block → Approval Workflow → Credit Block Release → Delivery

When the customer's credit exposure exceeded the available credit limit:

  • The Sales Order must be saved successfully.
  • The Sales Order must be placed under credit block.
  • A workflow must be triggered automatically.
  • The required approval level must be determined dynamically.
  • Approvals must be routed sequentially from L1 to L5.
  • After the final approval, the credit block must be automatically released.
  • If rejected, the Sales Order must remain blocked.

How the Approval Level Is Determined

The approval level was not fixed for every Sales Order. It was determined using:

Company Code + Credit Limit Exhausted Value

The Credit Limit Exhausted value was calculated as:

Credit Limit Exhausted = Sales Order Net Value − (Credit Limit − Credit Exposure)

For example:

ParameterValue
Credit Limit1,000,000
Existing Credit Exposure900,000
Sales Order Value250,000
Available Credit100,000
Credit Limit Exhausted150,000

The calculated value is then compared with the customer's DoA (Delegation of Authority) matrix to determine the required approval level.

For example:

Credit Limit ExhaustedApproval
0 – 25,000L1
25,001 – 100,000L2
100,001 – 250,000L3
250,001 – 500,000L4
> 500,000L5

The above ranges are illustrative. Actual thresholds are maintained based on the customer's Finance/Credit Management DoA matrix. 

Technical Approach

The workflow is triggered when the Sales Order is saved and the standard credit check results in a credit block. The implementation checks:

KNA1-KTOKD = 'XD01'
VBAK-CMGST = 'B'

The Sales Order number is then passed to the workflow. Before triggering a new workflow, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists for the same Sales Order. The required information is retrieved from SAP Credit Management and Sales Order data, including:

Sales Order Net ValueVBAK-NETWR
Credit Control AreaVBAK-KKBER
Credit SegmentUKM_KKBER2SGM
Business PartnerVBPA
Credit LimitUKMBP_CMS_SGM
Credit ExposureUKM_COMMTS_READ

The calculated Credit Limit Exhausted value is then used to determine the applicable approval level.

Approval Workflow

The approval follows a sequential process:

Sales Order
↓
Credit Limit Exceeded
↓
Credit Block
↓
Calculate Credit Limit Exhausted
↓
Determine DoA Level
↓
L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L5 Approvals
↓
Release Credit Block
↓
Delivery

Each approver receives the blocked Sales Order in the workflow inbox. If an approver rejects the request, the Sales Order remains blocked. The exact rejection and resubmission behaviour can be defined based on the customer's business process. After the final approval, the workflow automatically updates the credit status and releases the Sales Order from the credit block.

This implementation demonstrates how standard SAP Credit Management can be combined with SAP SD and workflow capabilities to handle credit-limit exceptions in a controlled manner. Instead of simply rejecting a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved, credit blocked, routed through the appropriate approval hierarchy, and automatically released after the required approval.

This approach provides a flexible and traceable solution for customer-specific credit approval requirements in SAP S/4HANA.

Testing and Challenges Faced

During testing, one of the important things to check was whether the workflow was triggered only when the Sales Order was credit blocked. Since users can save the same order multiple times, we also had to consider the possibility of duplicate workflow instances being created for the same Sales Order. To avoid this, the system checks whether an active workflow already exists before triggering a new one.

Another scenario to consider was a change in the Sales Order after approval. For example, if the order value increases after the approval is completed, the previously approved amount may no longer be sufficient. In such cases, the credit limit exhausted value needs to be recalculated, and the approval level must be determined again if the change affects the approval requirement.

Partial deliveries also need attention. Even if a Sales Order has been approved, the system should continue to follow the configured credit-check rules for subsequent delivery processing. The workflow approval should not automatically bypass any further credit checks required by the business.

These scenarios highlighted the importance of checking not only whether the workflow works correctly, but also whether the credit status remains consistent throughout the Sales Order process.

What I Would Improve

One thing I would focus on is keeping the approval-level determination separate from the workflow logic. Since the approval level depends on the company code and the credit limit exhausted value, maintaining the DoA thresholds in a configurable table would make future changes easier.

I would also give more attention to Sales Order changes after approval. Recalculating the exhausted value before releasing the credit block helps ensure that the approval is still valid for the current order. This is particularly important when the order value or the customer's credit exposure changes while the workflow is in progress.

Conclusion

Implementing this requirement helped demonstrate how SAP Credit Management and SAP Business Workflow can work together to handle credit-limit exceptions. Instead of preventing users from saving a Sales Order when the credit limit is exceeded, the order can be saved and kept blocked until the required approval is completed.

The main advantage of the five-level approval process is that the approval authority is determined based on the actual credit limit exhausted value rather than following the same approval route for every order. Although this requires additional workflow logic and testing, it provides better control over credit exposure and supports the customer's DoA requirements.

Before implementing a similar solution, it is important to define the approval thresholds clearly and consider scenarios such as order changes, partial deliveries, rejection, and changes in credit exposure. These details help ensure that the credit block is released only when the required business conditions are satisfied.

entry.title: Clearing SE16N Buffer After Table Structure Changes
entry.content:
Introduction

While working on custom developments, we often modify database tables after they have already been used in transactions such as SE16N. In one of my recent developments, I increased the length of a field in a custom table. Although the table was activated successfully and the database adjustment was completed, SE16N continued to display the old field length.

This blog explains why this behavior occurs and how it can be resolved using a standard SAP program.

 

I created a custom database table ZPOOJ_DB_BLOG_TB in SE11 with three fields. The Email field was initially defined with a length of 5.

Initial Table Definition

 Custom table with Email field length 5

At this stage, the table was activated and some test data was maintained.

To allow future enhancements, I changed the Enhancement Category to "Can be Enhanced (Deep)" and activated the table.

After that, I used SE16N to maintain table entries.

Data Maintenance in SE16N

SE16N allowing only 5 characters for Email field

 


As expected, the Email field allowed only five characters.

Requirement Change

Later, a requirement came in to increase the Email field length from 5 to 25 characters.

I modified the corresponding domain in SE11 and activated the changes.

Modified Field Length

Email field length changed to 25

After activation, I adjusted the database table through SE14 to ensure the database structure was updated.

To verify the change, I maintained table contents using Utilities → Table Contents.

Verification Through Table Contents

Email field accepting 25 characters

The updated field length was working correctly.

Issue Observed

However, when I returned to SE16N and tried to create or modify entries, the Email field still allowed only five characters.

Issue in SE16N

SE16N still showing old field length

At first glance, it appeared as though the field length change had not been applied. However, the database table was already updated correctly.

The reason for this behavior is that SE16N stores table metadata in its buffer. Since the table was accessed before the modification, SE16N continued to use the buffered information instead of reading the latest table definition.

Solution

SAP provides a standard report called BALVBUFDEL that clears the ALV buffer information.

Execute the report using transaction SE38.

Execute Standard Program BALVBUFDEL

Running BALVBUFDEL report

After executing the report, return to SE16N and test the table again.

Result After Buffer Refresh

Email field now accepting 25 characters in SE16N

The updated field length is now correctly reflected in SE16N.

Conclusion

When changes are made to the structure of a database table, such as increasing the length of a field, the changes may not immediately appear in SE16N even though the table has been activated and adjusted successfully.

In such situations, the issue is often caused by buffered metadata used by SE16N. Executing the standard SAP report BALVBUFDEL clears the buffer and forces SE16N to read the latest table definition.

This simple check can save significant troubleshooting time when table structure changes do not seem to be reflected in SE16N.

entry.title: Official Document Numbers (ODN) now replicated in Central Finance
entry.content:
As tax authorities worldwide tighten their grip on digital reporting, the document number on an invoice is no longer just an internal reference — it is a legally binding identifier that must flow accurately through every system in your landscape. SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 closes a critical gap for Central Finance customers by introducing Official Document Number (ODN) replication.

What Is an Official Document Number?

An Official Document Number (ODN) is a unique identifier that companies are legally required to assign to specific business documents — invoices, credit notes, and similar records — in accordance with rules set by government authorities. The format, length, and structure of an ODN vary by country and are strictly defined by regulators.

Until recently, SAP stored ODNs in standard reference fields on the accounting document (such as BKPF-XBLNR). These fields were too short for some countries' requirements, and customers frequently repurposed them for other business data. The ODN framework (available since S/4HANA 1709) introduced a dedicated storage structure — table GSLOG_LFD — with sufficient length, multi-value support per document, and a clear separation from other reference fields.

The Central Finance Challenge

Central Finance (CFIN) lets organizations replicate financial postings from one or more source ERP systems (S/4HANA or ECC) into a central S/4HANA hub — without replacing the source systems. This is a popular path for harmonizing statutory reporting while keeping existing operations running.

The challenge: when a document is replicated from source to Central Finance, it gets a new FI document number in the target system. Without additional handling, the ODN assigned in the source would be lost — leaving Central Finance with legally incomplete documents.

⚠️POLAND / KSeF DEADLINE

Poland's mandatory KSeF e-invoicing regime requires every invoice to carry a government-issued KSeF number. For companies running Central Finance, this number must be present in the CFIN system for statutory reporting — making ODN replication a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

How ODN Replication Works

SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS02 introduces native ODN replication as part of the Central Finance integration. The solution covers two main scenarios:

🔄Scenario 1 — Clearing Transfer (AP/AR Invoices)

AP/AR invoices — FI, SD billing, and MM — are posted in the source system where the ODN is assigned (for example, a KSeF number received from the Polish government via DRC e-invoicing). During replication to Central Finance, the ODN is carried across and persisted in GSLOG_LFD against the new CFIN FI document key, while traceability to the original source document number is maintained.

A document header can carry multiple ODNs — for example, a Poland invoice may hold both an individual KSeF number and a collective KSeF reference. All are replicated.

💳Scenario 2 — Central Payment

Invoices are posted in the source; the actual payment and clearing documents are created directly in Central Finance. For Poland, no ODN is currently legally required on the payment/clearing document itself. If a future jurisdiction mandates it, the ODN framework in CFIN is ready to assign one centrally.

Preservation vs. Assignment

The solution operates in two modes depending on configuration and legal requirement:

  • Preservation mode: The source ODN is validated and stored in CFIN unchanged. Target-side ODN generation is disabled for replicated documents to prevent the source number from being overwritten.
  • Assignment mode: If a document is created natively in CFIN (for example, a central payment) and a country requires an ODN, CFIN assigns one using its own ODN framework configuration and number ranges.

Source Coverage

  • S/4HANA source: ODNs are read from GSLOG_LFD (RECORD_TYPE = 'ODN') for document types ADH (FI header), BDH (SD billing header), and IDH (MM invoice header). All ODN fields — including timestamps and ODN type — are replicated unchanged.
  • ECC source: The ODN framework does not exist in ECC; country- or customer-specific extraction logic maps values into the CFIN ODN storage.
  • Initial load: Existing FI header ODN data can be back-filled together with the FI document initial load.

Why It Matters for Business

  1. Centralised compliance: If your statutory reporting runs out of Central Finance, ODNs flow automatically — no manual reconciliation between systems.
  2. Future-proof architecture: The ODN framework is country-agnostic by design. As more jurisdictions introduce mandatory document numbering, replication in Central Finance will be ready.
  3. Minimal disruption: Replicated ODN data is stored in the same database table used natively by the ODN framework (GSLOG_LFD). Consuming applications and statutory reports in Central Finance require little to no adjustment.
  4. Configuration safeguards: ODN number generation in Central Finance is disabled for replicated documents through customer configuration settings (by company code, document type, and further restrictions), preventing replicated numbers from being overwritten.

Availability

Get Ready for Poland — and What Comes Next

If your organisation uses Central Finance and operates in Poland, the time to plan is now. Here is a practical checklist to get started:

  • Verify that DRC e-invoicing is configured in your source systems to receive KSeF numbers from the Polish government.
  • Review ODN generation settings in Central Finance for replicated company codes and document types to prevent conflicts.
  • Scope the initial load for any existing documents that need to be back-filled before the 2026 reporting deadline.
  • For other countries using the ODN framework (Israel, Slovenia, Vietnam) or regions anticipating future mandates — no architectural rework is required; coverage can be extended incrementally.

For more information, visit the SAP Help Portal or reach out to your SAP account team.

entry.title: Performance optimization of XPRAS_AIMMRG phase of S4HANA upgrade
entry.content:
• Introduction
  • What is XPRAS_AIMMRG?
  • The Problem
  • The Reason
  • Where is the time spent?
  • What is getting converted?
  • Why does it take so much time?
  • Problem 1: Triggers
  • Problem 2: Partitions
  • The Solution
  • Triggers
  • Partitions
  • The Optimization
  • SHDB PFW
  • Resource Provider Optimization
  • Wait a min, if resource provider is monitoring and if the system is under utilized why is it ramping down?
  • Package Provider Optimization
  • Summary
  • Tools
  • References

 

Introduction

A decade into the S/4HANA era, release upgrades are routine, but the critical benchmark remains business downtime.

On a recent upgrade to S/4HANA 2023 FPS 04, our downtime phase blew out to 51 hours due to data conversion phases like XPRAS_AIMMRG. 

I got to be a part of an incredible team that completed an S4HANA upgrade from S42021 FPS 02 to S42023 FPS04 and achieved a 5x reduction of the technical downtime from when it started in development environment to production. 

SUM Execution phase duration across environments

 

The intended audience is SAP Basis Architects/Engineers and anyone curious!

This will be applicable for any release upgrade to S4HANA 2023 and higher.

I will be focusing on a very narrow and specific portion of the SUM upgrade downtime phase - Execution --> XPRAS_AIMMRG and how to optimize the SAP Parallelization FrameWork (PFW).

 

What is  XPRAS_AIMMRG?

XPRAS stands for eXecution of PRogram After Import, and the program is for application-related conversions, adjustments, data mergers or alignments for the conversion of release-specific SAP-shipped customizing that needs to be adjusted during the upgrade.

The important part relevant for this conversation is table(s) content is adjusted during this phase.

 

The Problem

The development system was a fresh copy of production and the SUM technical upgrade ran for 6 days with downtime phases running for 51 hours!

If you're asking, wait a min, development? Did you guys not practice in a POC environment first?  We did a POC for FPS03, but shifting timelines and project needs evolved.

Now back to the story...

Development System - SUM Duration breakdown

 In the 51 hours of SUM downtime, about 47 hours were spent in XPRAS_AIMMRG (Data Conversion)! approximately 92% of the total technical downtime!

This is in no way an acceptable runtime for our business.

Sure, the development system is not the same size hardware as production:  

EnvironmentApplication server compute Database compute
Development96 vCPUs, 360 GB Memory416 vCPUs, 9 TB Memory
Production176 vCPUs, 704 GB Memory1,920 vCPUs, 32 TB Memory

...but that is not the reason.

 

The Reason

Where is the time spent?

It was running longer for one specific XPRA - SAPR758XPRA90000126, if it's actively running the log will be located under /sapmnt/<SID>/SUM/abap/tmp/ . The majority of the time was spent on conversion of two specific Finance Asset Account tables:

  • FAAT_DOC_IT (Statistical Line Item in Asset Accounting) - ~44hrs
devhost:devadm 62> grep FAAT_DOC_IT SAPR758XPRA90000126.DEV | grep started | head -1 ;grep FAAT_DOC_IT SAPR758XPRA90000126.DEV | grep ended | tail -1
3 EPU468 XCLA "CL_XCLA_FAAT_DOC_IT": Editing of package "10" started - PID "5": "20250908195022"
3 EPU469 XCLA "CL_XCLA_FAAT_DOC_IT": Processing of package "3.849" ended - PID "5.068": "20250910155034"
  • FAAT_PLAN_VALUES (Planned Depreciations and Revaluations) - ~3 hrs
devhost:devadm 63> grep FAAT_PLAN SAPR758XPRA90000126.DEV | grep started | head -1 ; grep FAAT_PLAN SAPR758XPRA90000126.DEV | grep ended | tail -1
3 EPU468 XCLA "CL_XCLA_FAAT_PLAN_VALUES": Editing of package "3.889" started - PID "6": "20250908195047"
3 EPU469 XCLA "CL_XCLA_FAAT_PLAN_VALUES": Processing of package "12.852" ended - PID "1.471": "20250908224930"

 

What is getting converted?

Both tables are getting a new field RLDNR (Ledger in General Ledger Accounting) of data type CHAR(2) and that required adjusting the existing high volume of records.

The record count at the time of development system upgrade:

Table NameRecordsXPRAs Duration
FAAT_DOC_IT969,621,283~44 hrs
FAAT_PLAN_VALUES2,302,811,642~ 3 hrs

Important to note that the SQL statements for the update will be updating a view (as shown below) and not the direct table. 

UPDATE "Z09886V000010001" SET "LDGRP" = ? , "RLDNR" = ? WHERE "MANDT" = ? AND "BUKRS" = ? AND "ANLN1" = ? AND "ANLN2" = ? AND "GJAHR" = ? AND "AWTYP" = ? AND "AWREF" = ? AND "AWORG" = ? AND "AWSYS" = ? AND "SUBTA" = ? AND "AFABE" = ? AND "SLALITTYPE" = ? AND "DRCRK" = ?

 

Why does it take so much time?

Until you do the first system, there is no easy way to know in advance which tables are being adjusted in the XPRAs.

 

Problem 1: Triggers

SUM tool gives you a list of tables towards the end of the preprocessing phase MAIN_PREDTCHECKS/RUN_CHECK_DB_TRIGGER_PREDT (uptime), and the only tables we got were:
/OPT/VIM_1ITEM, COBRB, DD01L, DD02L, DD02T, DD03L, DD03T, DD04L, DD04T, DD07T, DFKKSUM, FEBKO, T002, T002T, T100, TRDIRT

We disabled/dropped triggers only for these tables.

So, when we did the analysis the first thing that stood out was that SLT triggers were still active for these two FAAT* tables and the AFTER UPDATE  triggers were constantly executing :

SUBJECT_TABLE_SCHEMASUBJECT_TABLE_NAMETRIGGER_NAMETRIGGER_ACTION_TIMETRIGGER_EVENT
SAPHANADBFAAT_DOC_IT/1LT/00008235INSAFTERINSERT
SAPHANADBFAAT_DOC_IT/1LT/00008235UPD1AFTERUPDATE
SAPHANADBFAAT_DOC_IT/1LT/00008235UPD2AFTERUPDATE
SAPHANADBFAAT_DOC_IT/1LT/00008235DELAFTERDELETE
SAPHANADBFAAT_PLAN_VALUES/1LT/00008236INSAFTERINSERT
SAPHANADBFAAT_PLAN_VALUES/1LT/00008236UPD1AFTERUPDATE
SAPHANADBFAAT_PLAN_VALUES/1LT/00008236UPD2AFTERUPDATE
SAPHANADBFAAT_PLAN_VALUES/1LT/00008236DELAFTERDELETE

 

Problem 2: Partitions

If you noticed the table records, you are probably wondering why FAAT_PLAN_VALUES ran faster than FAAT_DOC_IT despite having more than double the total records. The answer is FAAT_PLAN_VALUES is partitioned while FAAT_DOC_IT was not.

Table NameRecordsXPRAs DurationPartitions
FAAT_DOC_IT969,621,283~44 hrs1
FAAT_PLAN_VALUES2,302,811,642~ 3 hrs56

The XPRAS - XCLA is executing multiple parallel update statements, which means constant locking, delta merges. When there is only a single partition of the table, then there is almost no parallelization.

 

The Solution

 

Triggers

The DB triggers have to be dropped or disabled because there is no way for the replication to catch up millions of changes; doing a full load of the table post upgrade is faster. The cleanest way is to disable the triggers from your SLT system as a part of the ramp down. 

However, if downtime has already started, the only option is to drop the triggers from DB level:

DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008235INS"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008235UPD1"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008235UPD2"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008235DEL"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008236INS"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008236UPD1"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008236UPD2"
DROP TRIGGER "/1LT/00008236DEL"
