https://me.sap.com/notes/2755741Potential Impact of SLT During SAP S/4HANA System Conversion / Upgrade of S/4HANA System

 

Partitions

FAAT_DOC_IT was partitioned based on the production usage, i.e how the business is using it in reads and writes - 3 HASH (AFABE) and 7 RANGE(GJAHR) = 21 partitions.

The next QA1 upgrade had significant improvement in the technical downtime. Total downtime is only ~8 hours and the breakdown is: 

Table NameRecordsXPRA DurationPartitions
FAAT_DOC_IT764,411,1665:30:0021
FAAT_PLAN_VALUES1,679,693,5742:47:4056

* QA1 FAAT_DOC_IT has ~200M records lesser than DEV, so for a fair comparison if we measure how long DEV take to process the first 764M records, its approximately 33 hours. The record count fluctuated less starting from QA1 onwards, so its immaterial to adjust the durations after QA1. 

** QA1 was the latest copy of production at that point in time it was refreshed (after dev upgrade), however planned data purge and archiving activity resulted in lower records. 

SUM QA1 duration breakdown

The major improvement is from FAAT_DOC_IT where we gained 83% reduction in runtime.

XPRA Duration Comparison for FAAT* tables

 

 

What about the QA hardware? It was exact same as dev, so the gain was from the above two fixes.

EnvironmentApplication server compute Database compute
Development96 vCPUs, 360 GB Memory416 vCPUs, 9 TB Memory
QA196 vCPUs, 360 GB Memory416 vCPUs, 9 TB Memory
Production176 vCPUs, 704 GB Memory1,920 vCPUs, 32 TB Memory

We iterated testing a couple of permutations  with the following:

  • Log mode normal v overwrite
  • AUTOMERGE ON v OFF

We settled on leaving Log mode normal and AUTOMERGE ON.

Then looking back at the UPDATE SQL WHERE clause and the current partition criteria, we realized it's not efficient. So, we decided to re-partition (HASH on ANLN1) the table iteratively and measured the runtimes.

TableHash 8 ANLN1Hash 16 ANLN1Hash 32 ANLN1Hash 64 ANLN1Hash 32 ANLN1
FAAT_DOC_IT18899667573
FAAT_PLAN_VALUES11160586557

At 64 partitions, the performance started to degrade(🔺), so it was evident we should go with 32 partitions - HASH 32 ANLN1

It worked well in QA HW, however when we practiced in the staging hardware which is identical to production, we noticed regression (took ~130 mins for each FAAT* table). X4 32 TB bare metals have 16 NUMA nodes, so we decided on 16 partitions (⭐) with each partition distributed per NUMA node.

XPRAs duration per partition strategy

 

Crucially, we had to ensure that the time spent re-partitioning did not erase our net performance gains. If you think about it, the partition strategy (ANLN1) is specific for the upgrade, the business usage is different so we have to re-partition twice - once before and once after SUM downtime to ensure smooth business operations after go-live.

So, we deployed every optimization at our disposal to complete the re-partitioning in less than 30 mins, set the cutover task of re-partition to happen in parallel to the DB backup that runs at the beginning and end of the downtime. 

 So, we have a solution....

We are done right?

 

The Optimization 

While the solution did improve the performance, we observed a few things:

  • The DB resources were underutilized, CPU utilization was ~5%, despite being DB heavy operational phase(all are UPDATEs). 
  • At any given time the total parallel UPDATE statements executing were <=12
  • There was an odd pattern of execution -
    • nothing executes
    • system resource usage metric sqls
    • no. of parallel statements starts at a lower value and then increases up to 4-12
    • repeat
  • The default package size is 250k records
  • FAAT_PLAN_VALUES is always the short pole, so the focus should be on FAAT_DOC_IT

An example from one of the QA runs:

  • When we plotted the start time of each package we could clearly see there were periods where nothing is running. 
  • Only about 4 instances where 10+ parallel executions occurred, each execution processing a package of 250k records (10*250k = 2.5M, a drop in the bucket compared to the total records to be processed, 764M)

QA2: Ramp up and down of packages

  •  One would think perhaps the processing times were higher, nay. The max runtime of any package processed was sub 20 seconds

Processing duration of each package

It was evident there is a lot of room for further improvement.

You can also get similar information from the SHDB PFW Traces, a GANTT chart showing the parallel execution:

PFW Task execution comparison with and without optimizations

 

To better understand this, here is a quick background on PFW!

SHDB PFW

Unlike typical SUM phases, during XPRAs, the CL_XCLA_FAAT_DOC_IT and CL_XCLA_FAAT_PLAN_VALUES operations utilize SAP's SHDB  Parallelization FrameWork (in short PFW).  This is not controlled by the SUM parameters under SUM utilities.

The framework is from factory class CL_SHDB_PFW_FACTORY and uses CL_SHDB_PFW_CONFIG to define parameters.

The PFW has four components:

Package Provider:  responsible for automatically dividing the total dataset into smaller, processable packages according to configurable rules.

Resource Provider: actively monitors the system's memory and process utilization to determine the maximum allowed number of parallel tasks, thereby preventing system overloads.

Parallelizer:   calls the application-specific logic for each package in a separate aRFC task

Dispatcher: coordinates the entire process by requesting packages and resources and launching the asynchronous tasks.

 

Resource Provider Optimization 

The first thing we tried was to increase the MAX_ABAP_WP parameter of CL_SHDB_PFW_CONFIG, from default 12 to 20. It did not work at all.

UPDATE SHDB_PFW_CONF SET value = 20, changeable = 'N'  WHERE appl_name = 'XCLA_PROCESSING' AND component = 'RESOURCE PROVIDER' and param = 'ABAP_MAX_WP';

What we learned is

  • The Resource provider of the PFW observes the system performance and constantly ramps up and down up to the max ceiling defined in ABAP_MAX_WP (refer to the plot where nothing was running for brief periods)
  • Per note 3514930, we disabled the RAMP_UP_WP  control of the Resource Provider
  • It is important to note there is a risk of DeltaRolloverLocks on the HANA DB when RAMP_UP_WP  is disabled, but we did not encounter this.
  • In combination with this, we iteratively increased to MAX_ABAP_WP=32
  • It worked but only a little, an overall gain of ~25 mins
--Disable ramp up by resource provider per note 3514930,
UPSERT SHDB_PFW_CONF (CLIENT, APPL_NAME, COMPONENT, PARAM, TYPE, LENGTH, VALUE, CHANGEABLE)
VALUES ('100', 'XCLA_PROCESSING', 'RESOURCE PROVIDER','RAMP_UP_WP', 'C','2',' ','N')
WHERE APPL_NAME = 'XCLA_PROCESSING' AND PARAM = 'RAMP_UP_WP';

Wait a min, if resource provider is monitoring and if the system is under utilized why is it ramping down?

The answer was in the PFW trace of Resource Provider (you can download from transaction SHDB_PFW_SUPPORT). Due to a bug Resource Provider was unable to collect the metrics and would retry for ~3mins before moving on. 

PackSel 2338 wait up to 880s for collector
WARNING: Collector provided invalid raw_delta values for SAPHANADB.FAAT_DOC_IT[25]
WARNING: Collector provided invalid raw_main values for SAPHANADB.FAAT_DOC_IT[25]
WARNING: Collector provided invalid raw_main_and_delta values for SAPHANADB.FAAT_DOC_IT[25]
WARNING: Collector provided invalid mem_usage_pct values for SAPHANADB.FAAT_DOC_IT[25]
WARNING: Collector provided invalid cpu_usage_pct values for SAPHANADB.FAAT_DOC_IT[25]
PackSel 2338 wait up to 880s for collector

 The fix is to disable the resource provider metric collection parameter DB_RESOURCE_CONTROL_DISABLED (Note 3683678)

UPSERT SHDB_PFW_CONF (CLIENT, APPL_NAME, COMPONENT, PARAM, TYPE, LENGTH, VALUE, CHANGEABLE) VALUES ( '000' , 'XCLA_PROCESSING', 'RESOURCE PROVIDER', 'DB_RESOURCE_CONTROL_DISABLED', 'C', 2, 'X', 'N' ) WHERE APPL_NAME = 'XCLA_PROCESSING' AND PARAM = 'DB_RESOURCE_CONTROL_DISABLED';
  • This cut our runtimes in half

Package Provider Optimization

  • The PARTITION_STRIPING  config of the Package Provider distributes the database load of parallel processes over several table partitions. The number of partitions that are simultaneously loaded by the parallel processes is fixed at 5. (Notes 3227915, 3231259).  We set the MAX_PART_STRIPING_CATEGORIES=0 to make it efficient i.e create one partition category for each existing partition.
INSERT INTO SHDB_PFW_CONF (CLIENT, APPL_NAME,COMPONENT,PARAM,TYPE,LENGTH,DECIMALS,VALUE,CHANGEABLE) VALUES ('000', 'XCLA_PROCESSING','PACKAGE PROVIDER','MAX_PART_STRIPING_CATEGORIES','I',4,0,'0','N');
  • Next we iterated through different package sizes to identify the optimum record count (Note 2723534).
    • Lower package sizes caused regression (100k records took longer)
    • Runtimes improved for higher package sizes up to 4 million records
    • Any package size higher than 4M records failed with data integrity issues i.e. did not process all the records
    • The data integrity failures are visible only in the XPRA logs, the SUM phase did not stop with an error. When we shared this with SAP, their response was this will be reported in longpost.log and then we take it forward with corresponding product support.  That is not useful advice, as the last thing you want to deal with is data integrity issues after an upgrade. It will cause unpredictable extension of downtime.
UPDATE SHDB_PFW_CONF SET value = [{"TABNAME":"VXCLAFAATPLANVAL","SIZE":4000000},{"TABNAME":"VXCLAFAATDOCIT","SIZE":4000000},{"TABNAME":"FAAT_PLAN_VALUES","SIZE": 4000000},{"TABNAME":"FAAT_DOC_IT ","SIZE":4000000},{"TABNAME":".{0,}","SIZE":250000}] changeable = 'N'  WHERE appl_name = 'XCLA_PROCESSING' AND component = 'PACKAGE PROVIDER' and param = 'OVERWRITE_PACKAGE_SIZE';

Processing duration per package size

 

Summary

The combined optimization efforts (triggers, partitioning, PFW tuning) reduced the XPRA processing of the table FAAT_DOC_IT to 31 mins from 330 mins. 

All optimizations applied the hardware was still barely used, the lesson here is that PFW can be tuned for efficiency without the need for better hardware.

We iterated the SUM downtime across 30+ runs to achieve the optimal runtime, I have condensed the iterations to a few key milestones for brevity. This was only possible because of a team that shared the same vision and curiosity. 

Summary of optimizations

 

 

Tools

  • The changes to PFW had to be done before XPRAs start, so add Breakpoint to XPRAS_AIMMRG
  • Transaction SHDB_PFW_SUPPORT supports tracing and also changing the configuration parameters, although executing SQLs is faster.
  • The XPRA log contains enough information to derive your insights

 

References

https://me.sap.com/notes/3514930/EWhy does the SHDB Parallelization Framework use fewer processes than configured
https://me.sap.com/notes/3227915PFW: activate PartitionStriping as default for all PFW-applications
https://me.sap.com/notes/3231259PFW: configurable number of partition striping categories
https://me.sap.com/notes/3683678/EPFW Resource Collector
https://me.sap.com/notes/2723534XCLA Framework: Allow package size modification

entry.title: "CSRF token is invalid" with a valid token: five things I learned reading the OData V4 CSRF check
entry.content:
Introduction

For most of my 16 years with ABAP, CSRF in OData was a ritual, not a topic: GET with x-csrf-token: Fetch, copy the token, send it back on the POST. Done.

Then the same question started showing up again and again in the Community: a POST to an ABAP OData V4 service works in Postman and fails everywhere else (CPI, a custom client, a script) with

"code": "/IWBEP/CM_V4H_RUN/042",
"message": "CSRF token is invalid",
"@SAP__common.ExceptionCategory": "CSRF_Token_Missing"

The token is right there in the request. So what is the server actually checking? I went into the standard code of two lab systems, S/4HANA 2020 and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758), read-only, and followed the check from the ICF handler down to the kernel side. Everything below comes from that code.

The setup

The happy path is two calls:

  1. GET with x-csrf-token: Fetch. The answer brings the token in the x-csrf-token header and, very often, a set-cookie: sap-XSRF_<SID>_<client>=...
  2. POST with x-csrf-token: <token>.

The V4 entry point is /IWBEP/CL_OD_HTTP_REQ_HANDLER. Its HANDLE_REQUEST calls HANDLE_CSRF_TOKEN_INT before anything else, so a CSRF failure never reaches your provider class.

Thing 1: 043 and 042 are different problems, and the category will not tell you which

  • No x-csrf-token header on the POST: 043 "CSRF token is missing".
  • Header present but the validation fails, for any reason: 042 "CSRF token is invalid".

In the 2023 code, every CSRF failure gets the exception category CSRF_Token_Missing, including the 042. So when you see "invalid" together with "Missing", nothing is contradictory: read the message number, not the category.

Thing 2: the check is not Gateway, it is ICF

Gateway only calls IF_HTTP_SERVER~VALIDATE_XSRF_TOKEN. The real logic is in CL_HTTP_SERVER_NET, and it has two modes:

  • With an HTTP security session (cookie SAP_SESSIONID_<SID>_<client>😞 the token is compared with the one stored in that session.
  • Without a security session: the server looks for the cookie sap-XSRF_<SID>_<client>. That cookie carries the token, a timestamp and an HMAC. The HMAC is recalculated from the token you send, the timestamp in the cookie and your user, and has to match.

If your GET answered with set-cookie: sap-XSRF_..., you are in the second mode. In the code, that cookie is only created when there is no security session holding a token.

Thing 3: the token alone is worth nothing

In the second mode, a request that has the token but not the sap-XSRF_<SID>_<client> cookie ends in cookie_not_found, and that becomes 042.

That is the whole Postman mystery: Postman keeps a cookie jar and sends the cookie back without telling you. Your iFlow or script sends the token and forgets the cookie.

The cookie sap-usercontext, which people often copy around, plays no part in this check.

Thing 4: what the pair depends on (and what it does not)

partwhat the check uses
useryes: it is inside the HMAC, so GET and POST must run with the same user
client and systemyes: they are in the cookie name
URLno: the cookie has path / and the URL is not part of the HMAC, so a fetch on the service root is fine for a POST on an entity set
age2020: under 24 hours; 2023: no time check in the code
pairingthe token and the cookie must come from the SAME fetch

So these also give 042: GET and POST with different users, different clients, or a token from one fetch combined with the cookie from another.

Thing 5: there is no switch for V4

For V2, the hub handler reads the SICF service parameter ~CHECK_CSRF_TOKEN, and 0 turns the check off (useful for a quick diagnosis). The V4 handler does not read it, or any other parameter. In both releases I checked, there is no SICF key for V4. Fixing the client is the only way.

When you are stuck, the ICF developer trace tells you exactly which case you hit, for example "No xsrf cookie found". In 2023 the reason also goes to the connectivity trace.

A quick checklist

what you see on the POSTlikely causefix
043 missingno x-csrf-token headersend the token header
042 invalid, GET returned sap-XSRF_...cookie not sent backsend Cookie: sap-XSRF_<SID>_<client>=<value> (only name=value, no path or flags)
042 after it worked beforedifferent user or client between GET and POSTsame credentials and same sap-client on both calls
042 in a loop or with retriestoken and cookie from different fetcheskeep the pair together

On the client side, make sure the POST really sends the Cookie header: in CPI's HTTP adapter it has to be allowed in the request headers. I verified only the ABAP side; check the CSRF and session options of your adapter version.

Conclusion

The error message is honest, just incomplete: "invalid" usually means "I cannot validate it", and the missing piece is a cookie you never looked at. Security checks are like that: when they fail quietly in the right place, they protect you; when you don't know where that place is, they cost you a day.

Next time you see 042, look at the set-cookie of your GET before you look at the token.

Which client gave you the most trouble with CSRF tokens?

entry.title: SAP PM: як не допустити, щоб поламане обладнання зупинило бізнес
entry.content:
🏷 Обслуговування / SAP PM

Зупинка виробничої лінії через поломку обладнання — один із найдорожчих сценаріїв для промислового підприємства. За даними Deloitte, незапланований простій коштує виробнику в середньому $260,000 на годину. SAP PM (Plant Maintenance) — інструмент, що дозволяє перейти від реактивного до превентивного обслуговування.

Що таке SAP PM?

SAP PM (Plant Maintenance), в S/4HANA перейменований на SAP EAM (Enterprise Asset Management), — модуль для управління технічним обслуговуванням та ремонтом обладнання. Він охоплює повний lifecycle активу: від введення в експлуатацію до списання.

Три стратегії обслуговування в SAP PM

•       Reactive Maintenance (аварійне) — обслуговування після поломки. Дорого і непередбачувано

•       Preventive Maintenance (планово-попереджувальне) — регулярне обслуговування за часовим або лічильниковим графіком

•       Predictive Maintenance (предиктивне) — обслуговування на основі реальних даних про стан обладнання (IoT, датчики). Найефективніше, але вимагає зрілої інфраструктури

💡 Тренд: SAP активно розвиває інтеграцію PM з IoT-даними через SAP IoT та AI. Датчики на обладнанні в реальному часі передають дані в SAP, який сам пропонує оптимальний момент для обслуговування — ще до виникнення аварії.

Ключові об'єкти SAP PM

•       Functional Location — місце розташування обладнання (завод, цех, лінія)

•       Equipment — конкретна одиниця обладнання з технічними характеристиками та документами

•       Maintenance Plan — план технічного обслуговування: що, коли і як обслуговувати

•       Maintenance Order — наряд на ремонт або ТО з плануванням матеріалів і трудовитрат

•       Notification — повідомлення про несправність від оператора або датчика

Інтеграція PM із суміжними модулями

SAP PM тісно пов'язаний із MM (запасні частини та матеріали для ТО), CO (облік витрат на обслуговування), PP (планування простоїв обладнання) та FI-AA (облік ремонтів як покращень основних засобів). Ця інтеграція дозволяє отримати повну картину вартості утримання кожного активу.

Хто виграє від SAP PM?

Промислові підприємства, енергетичні компанії, транспортні оператори, нерухомість із великим парком обладнання. Будь-яка організація, де простій обладнання безпосередньо впливає на виручку або безпеку, отримає відчутну віддачу від впровадження SAP PM.

🏷 #SAP #SAPPM #PlantMaintenance #AssetManagement #EAM #SAPЦікавинки #Maintenance

entry.title: Building an MCP Server for SAP S/4HANA on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Consider a routine business question: "How many sales orders did this customer place this year?" The answer already exists in SAP S/4HANA, yet obtaining it typically involves opening the right application, setting filters, exporting a list and counting the rows. The data is available, but the path to it is designed for experienced SAP users.

The solution described in this article provides a simpler path: a question goes in, and the answer comes straight from the system. Rather than adding another point-to-point integration, it places a single, well-defined layer in front of SAP S/4HANA: an MCP server. The server offers a small set of clearly described, read-only tools (count sales orders, find a business partner, show a cost center) and performs all SAP communication itself, using only released OData APIs and standard SAP BTP connectivity.

In the current implementation, a chat application calls these tools through a built-in, rule-based mode. No language model is involved, and every answer is built directly from SAP data.

All configuration is described generically. No system names, URLs, client numbers, IDs or credentials are included, so the approach can be mapped onto any landscape.

MCP at a Glance

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting applications to tools and data. An MCP server publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a description and parameters. A client (a chat application, an assistant or an agent platform) picks the right tool for a question, calls it and shows the result.

For SAP, this means the SAP logic is built once, in one governed place, and any MCP-capable client can reuse it. Clients can only call what the server publishes, nothing more.

Solution Architecture

No client communicates with SAP S/4HANA directly. Clients only call tools on the MCP server, and the server reaches the backend through standard SAP BTP services.

The client calls the MCP server; the server resolves the target system through the Destination service and reaches it through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector.

Layer Component Responsibility

ClientChat application (or any MCP client)Receives the question, selects a tool, presents the answer
ToolsMCP server (Python application)Offers S/4HANA data as read-only tools
RuntimeSAP BTP, Cloud FoundryHosts the MCP server
ConfigurationDestination serviceStores the target system's address and logon, outside the code
NetworkConnectivity service + Cloud ConnectorSecurely tunnels requests from SAP BTP into the on-premise network
BackendSAP S/4HANAProvides data through released OData V2 APIs

Connectivity to SAP S/4HANA

On SAP BTP, the MCP server reaches SAP S/4HANA in the standard way: it reads the target system from a destination, and every request travels through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector into the on-premise network. The server holds no SAP host names or passwords; both live in the destination.

For local development, the same server can call a test system directly with a technical user over VPN. No code change is needed to switch between the two.

Cloud Connector Configuration

One system mapping is sufficient. Exposing only the OData path keeps every other path on the system unreachable from SAP BTP.

Setting Value

Back-end typeABAP System
ProtocolHTTPS
Internal host / port<S/4HANA host> / <HTTPS port>
Virtual host / port<virtual host> / <virtual port>
Resource (URL path)/sap/opu/odata/ with "Path and all sub-paths"

Destination Configuration

The destination is created once in the SAP BTP cockpit (Connectivity → Destinations). A password change for the technical user is made here and requires no redeployment.

Field Value

Name<destination name>
TypeHTTP
URLhttp://<virtual host>:<virtual port>
Proxy TypeOnPremise
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication (technical user with read authorizations)
Additional propertysap-client = <client>
Location IDOnly if the Cloud Connector uses one

Request Flow

  1. A client calls a tool on the MCP server.
  2. The server reads the destination (cached for a few minutes) to learn where the system is and how to log on.
  3. The request goes through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector to SAP S/4HANA.
  4. SAP returns the data through the released OData API, and the server passes a clean result back to the client.

Tool Design

Clients choose tools by their names and descriptions, so these are written as carefully as the logic behind them.

Business-Specific Tools

The most frequent questions have their own tools:

  • Business partners: search by name, count, show details and addresses.
  • Sales orders: list, count, show one order with its items.
  • Cost centers: search, count, show details, and actual costs per G/L account or period.

Three rules apply to all of them:

  • Counts come from SAP. "How many…?" questions use dedicated count tools that ask SAP for the exact total instead of downloading and counting rows.
  • Lists always state the real total. A list shows at most a few hundred rows, but always begins with "Total in SAP: N (showing M)", so a shortened list is never mistaken for the full result.
  • Nothing is assumed. Values such as the leading ledger or the current fiscal year are read from SAP at runtime, and IDs are always looked up, never guessed.

Generic Discovery Tools

For everything else, three read-only tools work on any allowed OData service:

  • List services: which SAP APIs may be used.
  • Describe a service: its entity sets and fields, with SAP's own field labels (read from $metadata).
  • Query a service: read rows with filters, always with the total number of matches.

Natural-Language Search Based on SAP Metadata

For questions that no specific tool covers, a search tool takes the question as plain text and works out the query on its own. It contains no hard-coded list of services or fields. Instead, it reads the metadata of every allowed service and matches the words in the question against SAP's own entity and field labels. For example, "maintenance notifications for plant 1000" is matched to the maintenance notification entity set, with a filter on the plant field.

Every result states exactly what was queried: service, entity set and filter. If the search picks the wrong data, the user can see why and rephrase. The search is deliberately simple, covering one entity set at a time with counts, filters, text search and sorting by latest or largest.

Service Governance and Allow-List

The generic tools work only on an allow-list of OData services. A default list is defined in the code, and two settings on the application change it without redeployment:

  • SAP_ALLOWED_SERVICES replaces the list.
  • SAP_EXTRA_SERVICES adds services to it.

The list was chosen with the help of a small inventory script. It reads the system's own service catalog (/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE), classifies every registered service as standard API, custom or other, and checks for each candidate whether its metadata responds and whether the technical user can read data. The result is a list of service names only, with no business data, which gives the SAP Basis team a clear, factual view of what is active, what fails and what is not available in the installed release.

The server also checks this catalog regularly and hides any tool whose service is not registered in the system. Once SAP Basis activates a service, its tools appear automatically, without a code change.

What SAP Basis Needs to Provide

Item Where

Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount, with the OData path exposedCloud Connector administration
A technical user with read authorizations: S_SERVICE for each allowed OData service, plus the business authorizations for the dataSU01 / PFCG
The required OData services activated/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE
Analysis of failing services (HTTP 500 and similar)/IWFND/ERROR_LOG
Later, for production: principal propagation, so each user sees only data their own SAP authorizations allowCloud Connector and SAP S/4HANA trust configuration

Deployment Steps

1. Implement the MCP Tools

The server is a small Python application built with the official MCP SDK. A tool is an ordinary function marked with @McP.tool():

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("S4HANA Server")

@mcp.tool()
async def count_sales_orders(customer: str = "") -> str:
    """Exact NUMBER of SAP sales orders. Give 'customer' (sold-to party) to count only theirs."""
    flt = f"SoldToParty eq '{customer}'" if customer else ""
    total = await sap_count("API_SALES_ORDER_SRV", "A_SalesOrder", flt)
    return f"Count of sales orders: {total}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")
  • The docstring becomes the tool description that clients read to decide when to use it.
  • The parameters (here customer) become the tool's input schema.
  • sap_count is a small helper that calls the OData service through the destination and asks SAP only for the total ($inlinecount=allpages with $top=1), so no rows are downloaded.
  • mcp.run starts the server over HTTP, which is how it runs on SAP BTP. For local testing it can run over standard input/output instead.
pip install "mcp[cli]" httpx

2. Create the BTP Service Instances

cf create-service destination lite <destination-instance>
cf create-service connectivity lite <connectivity-instance>
cf cups <secrets-instance> -p secrets.json      # holds the MCP access key; delete the file afterwards

3. Describe the Application

A short manifest.yml binds the three services and keeps writes switched off:

applications:
  - name: <mcp-app>
    buildpacks: [python_buildpack]
    memory: 256M
    command: python server.py
    services: [<destination-instance>, <connectivity-instance>, <secrets-instance>]
    env:
      MCP_TRANSPORT: http
      SAP_ALLOW_WRITES: "false"

4. Deploy

The destination name is set once as an application setting, so the repository contains no system-specific values:

cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com --sso
cf set-env <mcp-app> SAP_DESTINATION <destination-name>   # once
cf push
cf logs <mcp-app> --recent

5. Verify

Before connecting the chat application, a test client lists the tools on the deployed server and runs each one against real data. Tools whose services are not activated should not appear in the list.

Challenges and Resolutions

Challenge Root cause Resolution

"403 – No service found" for a standard APIThe service was not activated, or it was registered under a different technical name than its URL nameCall services by the URL name shown in the service catalog; activate missing services in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE
HTTP 406 when reading service metadataMetadata is only available as XML, but JSON was requestedRequest metadata as XML
HTTP 400 on certain analytical entity setsThese entity sets require mandatory parametersExclude them from the generic search; query them with their parameters
HTTP 500 on individual servicesService-side errors in the backendAnalysed by SAP Basis in /IWFND/ERROR_LOG
Empty results for some queriesMissing authorizations for the technical userCheck read access per service early with the inventory script
Errors on open-ended "valid to 9999-12-31" datesDate conversion overflow in the applicationFixed in the server's date handling
Slow responsesThe destination was read on every callCache the destination for a few minutes

Key Takeaways

  • MCP provides a clean integration layer for SAP: build the S/4HANA access once and reuse it from any MCP-capable client.
  • Clean core is maintained: released OData APIs, the Destination and Connectivity services and the Cloud Connector keep the solution upgrade-safe and easy to approve.
  • Access is governed through configuration: an allow-list, checked against the system's own catalog, exposes only what exists and what is permitted.
  • Read-only comes first: accurate answers build trust before any write scenario is considered.

Conclusion

Making SAP S/4HANA data accessible through simple questions requires neither replacing existing systems nor modifying the core. An MCP server in front of standard OData APIs, running on SAP BTP with standard connectivity, turns the system of record into a set of secure, well-described tools. Every figure in an answer comes directly from SAP.

The lasting value is a reusable integration layer: today a chat application uses it directly, and other MCP-capable clients can use the same layer tomorrow without any change on the SAP side.

Feedback and experiences from similar SAP S/4HANA integrations are welcome in the comments.

entry.title: SAP Datasphere Replication Flow Fails with CDS Views Having No Key Fields — What Actually Happens?
entry.content:
A CDS view can return valid data in SAP S/4HANA and still be unsuitable for a particular replication scenario in SAP Datasphere.

One issue I encountered while working with Finance data was a CDS source that did not expose the required key fields for replication. The source data was available, but the replication approach had constraints that needed to be addressed before the data could be consumed downstream.

Understanding the role of keys is essential to diagnosing this correctly.

1. Why does a Replication Flow require key fields?

A primary key uniquely identifies a record within a dataset. In replication scenarios, this identity becomes particularly important when the source supports inserts, updates, and deletes.

Consider the following source data:

Company CodeDocumentLine ItemAmount
1000190000010015,000
1000190000010023,000
1000190000020017,000

If the document number alone is treated as the key, the first two records cannot be uniquely identified. A suitable key might require a combination of company code, document number, fiscal year, and line item, depending on the source object's actual business grain.

Without a reliable record identity, the replication mechanism cannot safely apply record-level changes using an arbitrary key.

SAP documents this limitation in KBA 3531135.

2. What happens when the CDS view has no key?

When adding a source object to a Replication Flow, you may encounter an error similar to:

The following source objects are not supported because they do not have a primary key.

However, a missing primary key does not automatically mean that every replication scenario is unsupported.

SAP Datasphere supports certain CDS views and ODP source objects without primary keys under documented conditions. These sources are restricted to Initial Only loading in the applicable scenarios; Initial and Delta processing is not supported without the required key definition. See SAP KBA 3543361.

The distinction is important:

  • Initial Only: Loads the source data for that run without ongoing delta replication.

  • Initial and Delta: Performs the initial load and subsequently replicates supported changes.

  • Delta Only: Replicates subsequent changes without performing an initial full load.

The available options depend on the source connection, source object type, and extraction capabilities. A CDS view must also meet the relevant extraction prerequisites.

3. How should the issue be diagnosed?

Before changing the data model, validate the source and connection configuration.

Step 1: Verify the CDS definition

Inspect the CDS view's key fields and extraction annotations. Confirm that the view is supported for the intended replication scenario.

For ABAP CDS sources, delta-enabled extraction commonly requires appropriate @analytics.dataExtraction annotations, including change-data-capture configuration where applicable.

Step 2: Verify the connection type

The key definition visible through the ABAP Dictionary may differ from the definition exposed at the HANA database layer.

For example, SAP's documentation describes cases involving tables such as ACDOCA, where a key exists in the ABAP application dictionary but not at the HANA database layer. The selected connection type can therefore affect source-object validation.

See SAP KBA 3531135.

Step 3: Check the required load type

Determine whether the requirement is a one-time snapshot or ongoing synchronization.

If the source has no primary key and meets the documented prerequisites, Initial Only may be an option. If ongoing delta replication is mandatory, the source design or extraction approach may need to change.

4. What are the practical alternatives?

The correct solution depends on the source and business requirement.

  • Use Initial Only: Suitable when a one-time snapshot is sufficient, and the source meets SAP's prerequisites.

  • Use an appropriate extraction-enabled CDS view: Prefer a supported source that exposes the required key and delta semantics.

  • Use an appropriate ODP extractor: Consider an existing supported extractor when it provides the required business data and extraction behavior.

  • Use SLT where appropriate: For supported table-replication scenarios, configure the source table for SLT replication and consume it through the supported connection and container.

  • Redesign the source: If a custom CDS view is involved, review its grain, key definition, and extraction capabilities before using it as a replication source.

Do not introduce an arbitrary key merely to bypass validation. A concatenated or generated key is safe only if it is stable, unique at the actual record grain, and compatible with the replication mechanism. It does not, by itself, enable delta extraction.

5. Key takeaway

A CDS view being queryable does not guarantee that it is suitable for replication. The source must satisfy the extraction, key, and load-type requirements of the selected Replication Flow scenario.

Before troubleshooting downstream Datasphere views, validate the source object's replication compatibility first. This prevents modeling work from being built on an ingestion approach that cannot meet the required data consistency or refresh requirements.

Reference: SAP Help Portal — Select Source and Target Connections for Replication Flows

entry.title: How to Configure Alternative-Based Confirmation for Storage Location Substitution in SAP S/4HANA
entry.content:
Overview

When stock is unavailable in the preferred storage location, manually changing the source can delay order processing and create inconsistencies. SAP S/4HANA addresses this challenge through Advanced Available-to-Promise (aATP) and Alternative-Based Confirmation (ABC). In this article, I’ll walk through the SPRO and Fiori configuration required to substitute storage locations automatically during sales order confirmation, followed by practical unit-test scenarios.

 

What You’ll Configure

  • Item category usages for ABC sourcing
  • Main-item and subitem behavior
  • Schedule line relevance for delivery
  • Characteristic combinations and substitution controls in Fiori
  • Unit tests for stock substitution and Backorder Processing (BOP)
 

Step 1: Complete the SPRO Configuration

Start in SPRO by configuring the enhanced check method for the applicable document purpose. Use the following IMG path:

Cross-Application Components → Advanced Available-to-Promise (aATP) → Configuration Activities for Enhanced Check Methods → Configure Enhanced Check Methods by Document Purpose

Define the ABC Item Category Usages

Usage

Description 

ABC0

ABC sourcing reset

ABC1

ABC sourc. main item

ABC2

ABC sourcing subitem

ABC4

Third-Party Direct Shipment

ABC5

Bought-In Item

Note: ABC storage location substitution requires subitem generation. The related item category and schedule line settings are described below.

 

Step 2: Define the Main Item and Subitem Categories

Create or identify two item categories: one for the ABC main item and one for the generated subitem.

Main item category: Use an item category that is not relevant for pricing, billing, or delivery. Standard item category TAPA can be used as a reference, but Billing Relevance must be blank. In this document, ZTA1 is used as the example main item category.

For the main item category, leave the following indicators unselected:

  • Billing relevance
  • Pricing
  • Item relev. for dlv

Select the indicator that allows schedule lines.

Subitem category: Use TAN or a copy of TAN, depending on the process requirements.

 

Step 3:Assign Item Categories to the ABC Usages

Assign item categories:  VOV4

 Item category maintained

ABC Sourcing Reset

For this item category usage, set the default item category to standard item (TAN). The higher-level item category should be the one you defined in the previous step ZTA1.

ABC Sourcing Main Item

For this item category usage, the default item category should be your sourcing item category ZTA1.

ABC Sourcing Subitem

The setting is the same as in sourcing reset. The default item category should be standard item (TAN). The higher-level item category should be your sourcing item category.

 

Step 4: Define and Assign Schedule Line Categories

For the main item category (ZTA1), assign a schedule line category such as CD and leave Item Relevant for Delivery unselected. This setting is critical because an incorrect delivery-relevance assignment can create inconsistencies in order processing and VA05 reporting, including orders that continue to appear open.

For the subitem category, assign the schedule line category required by your process and ensure that Item Relevant for Delivery is selected. The generated subitem must carry the confirmed quantity into delivery processing.

Path for Define and Assign Schedule Line Categories

Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Define Schedule Line Categories

Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Assign Schedule Line Categories

 

Step 5: Complete the SAP Fiori Configuration

After completing the SPRO settings, use the relevant SAP Fiori apps to define the characteristic combination, substitution strategy, alternative control, and location substitutions used by ABC.

SAP supports two app-based approaches for configuring storage-location substitution. Select the approach that matches your solution design, and then complete the following configuration sequence.

Use either the characteristic-combination-driven process or the applicable alternative-control process supported by your SAP S/4HANA release. In both cases, keep the determination attributes and substitution values aligned.

 

Below are 2 ways to achieve the Storage location substitution through APPS

1st possible process

2nd possible process

Step 5.1: Create characteristic combination

App- Manage Characteristic Combinations

Prerequisite

Create the characteristic combination and select the attributes that determine storage-location substitution. The exact characteristics depend on the business process; common examples include sales organization, distribution channel, plant, material, and the requested storage location.

  1. Enter a clear name and description for the characteristic combination.
  2. Set Usage to the application or process for which the characteristic combination is being defined.
  3. Set Catalog Type to the relevant business document or determination context.
  4. Add the required characteristics and use the Ordinal Number to define the sequence in which characteristic-value combinations are maintained and evaluated. 

Step 5.2:  Configure substitution strategy

APP-Configure substitution strategy

Create the substitution strategy that controls how ABC evaluates alternatives. Assign the relevant characteristic combination, define the evaluation sequence, and confirm that the strategy is active for the intended business context.

 

Step 5.3: Configure Alternative Control

APP-Configure Alternative Control

Activate the above combination in this step.

Assign the substitution strategy to the applicable alternative control and activate the characteristic-value combinations. Verify that the control is valid for the required document purpose and availability-check scenario.

 

Step 5.4: Manage Substitution - Locations

APP-Manage Substitution – Locations,

Maintain the permitted source and alternative storage locations for each characteristic-value combination. Confirm the priority sequence, validity dates, and activation status so that ABC can evaluate the alternatives in the intended order.

 

 

Step 6: Test the End-to-End Process

Create a sales order for a material whose preferred storage location does not have enough stock, while an allowed alternative location does. Run the availability check and verify that ABC generates the expected main-item and subitem structure, confirms the quantity from the alternative location, and leaves the main item non-delivery-relevant. Then create the delivery and confirm that only the subitem carries the deliverable quantity. Finally, review the order in VA05 and run the applicable Backorder Processing scenario to ensure that confirmations, item status, and closure behavior remain consistent.

 

Conclusion

By combining the SPRO item-category and schedule-line settings with the corresponding SAP Fiori configuration, aATP can automatically evaluate and substitute eligible storage locations during sales-order confirmation. The main item provides the sourcing structure, while the generated subitem carries the confirmed quantity through delivery processing. During testing, validate the confirmation result, item hierarchy, schedule-line relevance, delivery creation, and VA05 status so that the complete process works consistently from product availability through fulfillment.
