About the Author

Sukhbir Chhina is SAP SCM Solution Architect with experience across SAP SD, MM and PP. He translates complex supply chain requirements into scalable, integrated SAP S/4HANA solutions, with a focus on process architecture, cross-functional integration, solution governance, and delivery quality. His work helps organizations improve operational efficiency and build resilient, future-ready supply chains.

entry.title: From clean core level to decision: reading what a custom program actually does (part 3)
entry.content:
Disclosure: I'm the author of this post and the creator of Clean-Core.io, a free, non-commercial community tool. This post is educational and describes a method you can apply by hand; the tool is optional and complementary to SAP ADT/ATC and the SAP toolchain, not a replacement.

In part 1 we graded each dependency of a custom object on SAP's clean core levels A–D. In part 2 we turned that into visibility and two KPIs. Both answer how far a piece of code is from a clean core.

Neither answers the question that decides the effort: what does this program do for the business, and should it be kept, rebuilt or retired? This part is about reading that from the code.

The business rules are in the IF statements

A grown Z-program is often the only up-to-date description of a process. Two passages from a fictitious purchase requisition approval report:

"Plant 1000 is the central warehouse
IF gs_eban-werks = '1000'.        " line 87
  gv_skip_limit = abap_true.
ENDIF.

"Tolerance agreed with purchasing
IF lv_dev_pct > 5.               " line 412
  PERFORM hold_for_buyer.
  RETURN.
ENDIF.

Neither is a clean core violation. Both are business rules: plant 1000 skips the approval limit, and a price more than 5 % above the reference goes to a buyer. Whatever happens to the program, these two rules have to survive, or someone has to decide on purpose that they don't. No ATC check tells you that. The code does.

A reading flow

Step Look for Write down

1. Entry pointsSTART-OF-SELECTION, selection-screen events, dialog modules, public methods, function modulesthe line
2. Dataevery SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, MODIFY, DELETE on own or SAP tablesthe line, read or write
3. Business rulesIF / CASE on business values: plant, document type, amount, tolerancethe line, the condition in plain words
4. EffectsRFC, update tasks, BAPIs, mails, files, messagesthe line
5. Gapsdynamic calls with a variable target, includes you don't have"not determined", with the reason

Draw the result as a process. BPMN works well because a key user can read it. Anchor every task and gateway to its line: a step that can't point back to a line is an opinion, and a gap you write down is an open question rather than a wrong answer.

Then add what parts 1 and 2 gave you: each SAP object with its level and how it is used. Reading EBAN is a different matter from updating it; a direct write to an SAP table stays a problem whatever the table's own level. And run ATC in your system: it is the check that counts.

From the reading to a decision

Option When it fits

RetireNobody needs the process any more. Usage data helps here.
Move to SAP standardThe standard covers the process; each custom rule maps to configuration or is dropped on purpose.
RebuildThe rules are still needed. Rebuild in-app on ABAP Cloud where the logic belongs to the core, side-by-side on SAP BTP where it is loosely coupled or mainly talks to other systems.
Keep for nowWith the risk and a review date written down.

One thing that is easy to get wrong: a classic construct is not by itself a reason to move a program off the stack. A batch input, a piece of native SQL or a local RFC call is something to replace with a released API inside a rebuilt in-app solution. Side-by-side pays off when the logic itself is independent of the core, not because one statement is old.

Record which option you chose, on which evidence (the lines, the levels, ATC), under which assumptions, and who confirmed it. Six months later, that record is what makes the decision reviewable.

What the reading gives the next step

  • Target design: which SAP objects the new code reads through released APIs or CDS views. Part 1 used KNA1 → I_Customer; for EBAN, look up the released purchase requisition API for your release on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.
  • A first code draft that carries both rules over, for a developer to review in ADT and check with ATC and the Clean ABAP style guide.
  • Test cases from the same rules, so "plant 1000 skips the limit" is a test, not tribal knowledge.
  • The process as a BPMN 2.0 file for whoever documents the to-be process, for example in SAP Signavio.

Where this stops

  • The code shows the process the code implements. Customizing, jobs and manual steps around it are not in it.
  • Static reading can't resolve every dynamic call. Say so instead of guessing.
  • The levels come from SAP's published data; ATC in your target system has the final word.
  • Generated code, from any tool or model, is a draft for a developer to review.

Conclusion

Levels and scores tell you how far a program is from a clean core. The decision about the program needs one more thing: what it does, line by line, with its business rules made visible. Read that first, and "we have a lot of Z-code" turns into a list of decisions you can defend.

How do you get from a clean core level to a decision per program today: key-user workshops, a decision log, something else? And where has reading the code misled you?

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Group Reporting and SAP BDC: Why Replacing SEM-BCS Is More Than a Tool Change
entry.content:
For companies using SAP SEM-BCS, the end of maintenance for standard SAP BW is more than a system issue. They need to reorganize consolidation and their data architecture so that group financial statements, group planning, and corporate reporting as a whole continue to be based on consistent figures.

This article explains why Group Reporting is not merely a technical replacement, what roles SAP Datasphere and SAP BDC play in integrated corporate reporting, and what the business and IT teams should examine before making an architectural decision.

SAP’s Target Architecture: Group Reporting on a Common Data Foundation

Standard SAP BW is no longer at the center of SAP’s target architecture. SEM-BCS users therefore need both a new consolidation solution and a perspective for their BW-based data and reporting landscape.

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting handles consolidation, while SAP BDC exchanges master and transaction data between Enterprise Performance Management (EPM) applications, meaning solutions for consolidation, planning, reporting, and analysis. Only this connection turns the system change into integrated corporate reporting.

S/4HANA for Group Reporting: Consolidation Closer to Operational Finance

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting supports a wide range of group structures and consolidation scenarios with currency translation, intercompany eliminations, validations, journal entries, approvals, and audit trails. Its key advantage over an isolated solution is its proximity to operational FI/CO data.

Stand-Alone or ERP-Integrated: Two Paths for Consolidation

Group Reporting can run as stand-alone consolidation in a dedicated S/4HANA system or be integrated into the central S/4HANA system. Additional reported data can be incorporated via SAP Group Reporting Data Collection using forms, file uploads, APIs, or OData—including from non-SAP systems or for non-financial disclosures.

The decisive factor is how closely consolidation and operational accounting need to work together. The integrated option reduces system breaks in centralized S/4HANA landscapes; the stand-alone model offers greater flexibility with multiple ERP systems or separate responsibilities.

SAP Business Data Cloud Becomes the Integration Layer in Corporate Reporting

SAP BDC forms the data foundation of the EPM architecture. It combines data lake and data warehouse functions, exchanges master and transaction data between Group Reporting, SAP Analytics Cloud Planning, and other applications, and creates the basis for reports and dashboards.

 

For groups with multiple S/4HANA instances, the planned BDC data transfer layer is particularly relevant: It is intended to take transaction data from public- and private-cloud systems and transform it according to central rules. Mapping, derivation, substitution, and aggregation are performed in a controlled manner; the original data is retained.

This keeps transformations traceable and the origin of the figures visible. Large volumes of data can be processed in near real time; at the same time, this creates the foundation for continuous intercompany reconciliation at account level.

Data Products Provide Access—the Complete Reporting Logic Is Emerging Step by Step

Group Reporting content for master data and raw transaction data is already available for SAP Datasphere. Companies can use it to build their own models and reports. However, reporting items, rules, and the complete Group Reporting logic are not yet consistently covered as SAP-managed content in the BDC target architecture.

Companies therefore need to determine early on where the reporting logic resides, which models they will manage themselves in Datasphere, and which can later be supplemented by SAP content. Otherwise, old dependencies will simply migrate to a new platform.

 

 

New Functions Address Bottlenecks in the Financial Close Process

The functions introduced or announced for 2025 and 2026 address typical bottlenecks in the group financial close: Validations check reported data that has not yet been released, a Fiori app supports imports, prior periods can be reopened for release, and the consolidation monitor brings together the steps through to one-click consolidation.

Rule control is also becoming more granular: Entries can depend on entities, groups, or conditions; substitutions support capital consolidation, and configurable sign logic reduces external conversions. This means less file-based logic, clearer rules, and better auditability.

For 2026, planned developments include IFRS 18 updates, additional source fields and conditions in reporting rules, and improvements to Data Collection. Greater automation in portfolio and group structure management is intended to reduce maintenance effort and errors when structures change frequently.

Five Questions That Must Be Answered Before Choosing a Tool

  1. Which source systems supply reported data? Fully account for S/4HANA instances, non-SAP systems, non-financial data, and manual submissions.
  2. Where should consolidation be operated? Evaluate the stand-alone and ERP-integrated models in the context of governance and compliance, as well as release strategy and integration requirements.
  3. Which reporting logic must be retained? Document reporting items, rules, hierarchies, derivations, and special logic from SEM-BCS or BW.
  4. What belongs in Group Reporting, and what belongs in Datasphere? Clearly separate consolidation logic, data provisioning, and analytical models.
  5. Which roadmap functions are essential for the target architecture? Explicitly identify announced functions as dependencies and plan a robust interim solution.

A Sustainable Target Architecture Starts with the Process, Not the Product

The starting point is a functional assessment: Where do waiting times, manual rework, or gaps in traceability occur? This is used to create a prioritized process view.

Next, it is defined for each data source how it will be connected, transformed, and validated. Group Reporting Data Collection covers manual submissions as well as file-, API-, and OData-based submissions. SAP BDC and Datasphere handle data provisioning and modeling, while SAP Analytics Cloud provides reports, dashboards, and, depending on the scenario, group planning as well.

A phased implementation reduces risk: Start with a limited scope for the financial close and a small number of prioritized reports. Test data lineage, rules, validations, and the audit trail end to end before adding further entities, planning data, or non-financial information.

Conclusion: Replacing SEM-BCS Is Also an Architectural Decision

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting is more than the technical replacement for a consolidation landscape that is being phased out. Together with SAP Datasphere and SAP BDC, it can enable corporate reporting that connects financial data, consolidation, planning, and analysis on a common data foundation.

The benefits only emerge through clearly defined data flows, reporting logic, and responsibilities. The key question is therefore not, “Which tool will replace our current system?” but rather, “How do we create a financial close process in which every figure is quickly available, functionally explainable, and technically traceable?”

entry.title: SAP Green Ledger: Q3-26 Release Updates and Highlights
entry.content:
Welcome to the Q3 2026 edition of our SAP Green Ledger Quarterly Release Highlights! This blog summarizes the most important innovations and enhancements delivered for SAP Green Ledger during Q3 2026.

This quarter brought several new capabilities and enhancements to SAP Green Ledger, including faster master data imports with delta loads, new APIs for integrating carbon data from external sources, carbon allocations from energy flows, and more flexible GHG analysis. Further enhancements improve CBAM liability management and usability.

Read on to learn more about the key innovations introduced throughout Q3 2026: 

  • Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads 
  • API-Based Carbon Data Imports 
  • Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details
  • Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows
  • WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries 
  • Enhanced Carbon Liability Management 
  • More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 
  • Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 
  • Further Updates and Enhancements

 

Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads

The Manage Master Data Imports app now supports delta loads in addition to full loads when importing master data from a connected SAP S/4HANA system, enabling faster and more efficient master data imports. Instead of importing the complete master data scope with every import, a delta load imports only newly created and changed master data objects since the previous full or delta load. This reduces the amount of data that needs to be processed and can significantly shorten the time required for the import.

Delta Load Option for Master Data Import from Connected SAP S/4HANA System

Delta loads are currently supported for account, account hierarchy, product, and project master data in both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. For cost center master data, delta loads are currently supported for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Other master data objects continue to be imported in full, even when the import is started as a delta load. The first master data import is always performed as a full load. A full load may also be required for subsequent imports, for example when changes are made to the relevant business system.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Master Data.

 

API-Based Carbon Data Imports

SAP Green Ledger now provides three APIs for importing and processing carbon data from external sources. In addition to importing emission data from external sources via CSV files, the new APIs now provide a defined interface for integrating this data into SAP Green Ledger. The APIs support the different steps of the carbon data import process, from importing carbon data to releasing an import and monitoring its processing status.

The Carbon Data Import API allows you to import carbon data and create the data for the corresponding carbon collections. The Carbon Data Import Release API can then be used to release an import and trigger the creation of the corresponding carbon collections and journal entries. To monitor the process, the Carbon Data Import Status API provides information about the status of an import and the processing results of the corresponding carbon collections.

For more information, see the API Guide for SAP Green Ledger.

 

Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details

Once carbon data has been imported into SAP Green Ledger, it is important to understand how the data has been processed and what resulted from the import.

The Manage Carbon Data Imports app now provides more detailed information about your carbon data imports. You can review the imported data as well as the carbon collections and journal entries created from an import and navigate between them. This provides greater transparency into the results of a carbon data import and makes it easier to trace the imported data through to the resulting carbon collections and journal entries. The enhanced overview and navigation are available for new carbon data imports; existing imports remain unchanged.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Material Movements.

 

Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows

Energy flow models in SAP Sustainability Footprint Management represent how energy and the associated emissions are distributed across different elements of an organization. SAP Green Ledger now brings this information into carbon accounting to reflect the corresponding carbon allocations between cost centers. To support this, the import of modeled energy flows from SAP Sustainability Footprint Management has been extended. In addition to carbon emissions for energy sources, emissions for other nodes in the energy flow, such as facilities, meters, resources, and process infrastructures, are now also imported.

Using the Manage Carbon Data Imports app, you can import and release energy flows from a connected SAP Sustainability Footprint Management system. The imported data includes the cost center assignments of the individual nodes, which are carried into the corresponding carbon collections. When these carbon collections are posted to the journal, SAP Green Ledger creates the corresponding cost center-to-cost center allocations based on the modeled energy flow. The resulting journal entries include the respective cost centers and partner cost centers.

The carbon collections and resulting journal entries can be reviewed in the Manage Carbon Collections and Manage Journal Entries apps.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Energy Flows.

 

WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries

Carbon adjustments and corrections can now also be assigned to specific WBS elements when journal entries are created manually. The Manage Journal Entries app now supports WBS elements and partner WBS elements for manual journal entries.

When creating a manual journal entry, you can now assign a WBS element to a line item for eligible accounts. Cost center and WBS element are mutually exclusive and cannot be maintained for the same line item. When a WBS element is selected, the corresponding profit center and segment are automatically derived.

The WBS element value help displays WBS elements based on the relevant project and profit center context. The system also checks whether the selected WBS element is available for posting and informs you if any posting restrictions apply.

For more information, see SAP Help: Create Journal Entries.

 

Enhanced Carbon Liability Management

With the EU CBAM definitive regime in effect since January 2026, imports of certain goods into the European Union can result in carbon liabilities that need to be recognized and valued. SAP Green Ledger supports this process by accounting for the embedded emissions and the resulting carbon liabilities and by determining their fair value based on the corresponding certificate requirements and Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices. In Q3 2026, new enhancements provide further support for the valuation and review of these liabilities.

Official EU ETS Prices

The Configure Carbon Certificate Data app now displays the official quarterly ETS prices published by the European Union. These prices are automatically imported into SAP Green Ledger and used for the fair value calculation of carbon liabilities associated with imports subject to EU CBAM. You can view the official quarterly prices together with your maintained ETS prices in the Emissions Trading System Prices tab.

Official EU ETS Prices Imported for Quarter 1 and 2

A color indicator shows whether ETS prices are available for the current year and quarter: green indicates that prices are maintained for all calendar weeks, while blue indicates that the automatically imported official quarterly EU ETS prices are used.

For more information, see SAP Help: View and Maintain Emissions Trading System Prices.

Product Information in Carbon Liabilities

The Manage Carbon Liabilities app now displays the Product selected for carbon collections that require carbon certificates, providing additional context when reviewing carbon liabilities.

For more information, see SAP Help: View Carbon Liabilities and Create a Carbon Collection.

 

More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 

The Carbon Data Dashboard has been enhanced with new options for analyzing GHG emissions. 

The timing of GHG emission recognition can differ depending on whether emissions are considered when carbon data is posted or when the underlying resources are actually consumed. You can now choose between the accrual and non-accrual accounting method, which determines how GHG emissions are calculated and displayed in the dashboard. 

With the non-accrual method, GHG emissions are recognized when carbon-relevant data is posted to the GHG Liabilities Collection account. The resulting GHG emissions therefore represent the emissions recorded at the time of the carbon data posting, regardless of subsequent activities related to the underlying resources. 

With the accrual method, emissions are distinguished based on whether the underlying resources have already been consumed. Emissions related to consumed resources are recognized as realized GHG emissions in profit and loss accounts, while emissions related to resources that have not yet been consumed remain as accrued emissions in balance sheet accounts. As the resources are consumed, the corresponding emissions move from the balance sheet to profit and loss. This allows the dashboard to reflect GHG emissions in line with actual resource consumption.

Selection of Accrued and Non-Accrued GHG Emissions Overview

The Carbon Data Dashboard also introduces an enhancement to the WBS Element filter. The filter is now organized by project, with a project node at the top of the hierarchy grouping the corresponding WBS elements. This provides clearer context and makes it easier to locate and select WBS elements within their associated projects.

Enhanced WBS Element Filter Organized by Project

 For more information, see SAP Help: Analyze Carbon Data and Accounting Method.

 

Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 

The SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard has also been updated for Q3 2026 with enhancements to filtering and data visualization. The updates make it easier to analyze carbon data in the context of projects and WBS elements and further improve the presentation and interpretation of GHG and financial data. 

For a detailed overview of the latest SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard enhancements, see the dedicated SAP Community blog post and the SAP Help Portal topic Analyze Carbon Data Alongside Financial Data.

 

Further Updates and Enhancements

Several smaller enhancements further improve the usability of SAP Green Ledger. 

Line Item Totals and Subtotals 

The Line Items table in the Manage Journal Entries app now displays debit and credit totals and subtotals. When line items are grouped by an attribute, you can view the corresponding subtotals for each group, making it easier to analyze and review carbon-related postings. 

Filtering by Empty Dimension Values 

The Manage Journal Entries, Display Line Items, and Display Account Balances apps now allow you to filter for empty or unassigned values across supported dimensions, including, for example, WBS element, cost center, product, and supplier. You can display only postings where a particular dimension has not been assigned, or exclude these postings from the results. This makes it easier to review postings based on whether specific dimension information is available. 

Journal Entry IDs Without Leading Zeros 

Journal entry IDs are now displayed without leading zeros across SAP Green Ledger, making them easier to read, search, and sort. This applies wherever journal entry IDs are displayed. 

Documentation Feedback on SAP Help Portal

You can now provide feedback directly on the Admin Guide, Integration Guide, API Guide, and Introduction for SAP Green Ledger on SAP Help Portal. This makes it easier to share feedback on specific documentation content directly from the page you are viewing. For more information, see SAP Help: Giving Documentation Feedback on SAP Help Portal.

 

Additional Information 

If you want to dive deeper into SAP Green Ledger, the SAP Help Portal is a good place to start. It provides detailed information on concepts, configuration, and application usage. You can also check the What’s New section, which is updated with every release and gives a complete overview of the latest additions. To see what's coming next, the SAP Road Map Explorer offers insight into planned features and upcoming innovations. It is updated regularly and outlines how the solution will continue to evolve.

entry.title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones.

The configuration covered here implements TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store, allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

Prerequisites

  • Database certificate (.pfx format) signed by an external CA, plus the corresponding root certificate
  • Certificate password
  • Access to the HANA database server at OS level (sidadm or equivalent)
  • Access to all ABAP application server nodes at OS level
  • A valid HANA userstore key configured for hdbsql commands
  • Planned downtime or maintenance window — the ABAP application must be stopped during parts of this procedure
  • Existing SAPSSLS.pse backed up before making any changes

Overview

The procedure creates two sets of PSE (Personal Security Environment) files:

  1. SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA server — the HANA database server's SSL identity, built from the externally signed certificate. This is what HANA presents to the ABAP layer during the TLS handshake.

  2. sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse on each ABAP application server — these are placed in the sec directory of each ABAP node. They act as the trust store on the ABAP side, containing the CA certificate chain that the ABAP kernel uses to verify HANA's certificate. The sslKeyStore reference in the profile parameter also points to sapcli.pse, but since sslclientpki is off on HANA, the client certificate is never requested.

Step 1 — Upload Certificates to the HANA Server

  1. Log on to the HANA database server at OS level as sidadm
  2. Upload the database certificate (db_cert.pfx), the root certificate (root.cer) (and any intermediate certificates) to the sec directory on the HANA server:
/usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/global/security/rsecssls/

Note: The exact sec directory path may vary. Confirm the location using the SECUDIR environment variable.

  1. Before making any changes, back up the existing SAPSSLS.pse:
cp SAPSSLS.pse SAPSSLS.pse.bak

Step 2 — Create SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA Server

Run the following command to create a new SAPSSLS.pse from the externally signed certificate. This becomes the HANA server's SSL identity:

sapgenpse import_p12 -r root.cer -p SAPSSLS.pse <db_cert.pfx>
  • Enter the certificate password when prompted
  • When asked for a PIN, you have the option to set one or leave it empty. From a security perspective, setting a PIN is recommended as it adds an additional layer of protection to the PSE file. If a PIN is set, ensure it is stored securely as it will be required for any future PSE operations

SAPSSLS.pse should now be created successfully.

Step 3 — Create the Client PSE Files for ABAP Application Servers

sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse can be created directly from SAPSSLS.pse:

cp SAPSSLS.pse sapcli.pse
cp SAPSSLS.pse sapsrv.pse

Copy both files to the sec directory on every ABAP application server node (CS/CI and all additional application servers):

/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/

Step 4 — Disable sslclientpki on HANA

Important: Shut down the ABAP application layer before executing this step.

This parameter controls whether HANA enforces client PKI certificate authentication. Setting it to off enables one-way TLS (server authentication only), which is the configuration used here.

Run the following hdbsql command from the HANA server:

hdbsql -U <USERSTORE_KEY> "ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') SET ('communication', 'sslclientpki') = 'off' WITH RECONFIGURE;"

The WITH RECONFIGURE clause applies the change immediately without requiring a HANA restart.

PRD Systems: This parameter must also be disabled on the secondary/DR HANA node. This can be done via SAP HANA Studio — apply the change on both the primary and DR secondary database nodes.

Step 5 — Configure the ABAP Default Profile

The dbs/hdb/connect_property parameter must be added to the ABAP default profile (DEFAULT.PFL) to instruct the ABAP kernel to use SSL when connecting to HANA. This parameter applies to all application server instances.

Add the following parameter (adapt values to your system):

dbs/hdb/connect_property = ENCRYPT=TRUE,sslCryptoProvider=commoncrypto,sslKeyStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslTrustStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslHostNameInCertificate=<hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com>

Key values to adapt:

  • <SID> — your system ID
  • <instance_dir> — the instance directory of each application server (e.g. D00, D01)
  • <hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com> — the fully qualified hostname as it appears in the HANA certificate's CN/SAN field

Note: The sslHostNameInCertificate value must match exactly what is embedded in the HANA server certificate, otherwise the SSL handshake will fail.

Step 6 — Restart the Application and Validate

Start the ABAP application layer. Once all instances are up, perform the following validation steps.

Validation 1 — Check encrypted connections via SQL

Log on to the system and navigate to transaction DB02 → SQL Editor. Run the following statement, replacing <SCHEMA> with the correct database schema name:

SELECT IS_ENCRYPTED, SSL_VERSION, CLIENT_HOST
FROM SYS.M_CONNECTIONS
WHERE USER_NAME = '<SCHEMA>'
AND IS_ENCRYPTED = 'TRUE';

All active connections for the schema should return TRUE in the IS_ENCRYPTED column. If any sessions return FALSE, review the profile parameter and PSE file placement.

Validation 2 — R3trans connectivity check

Run the following from the OS level on each application server to confirm no transport-layer issues:

R3trans -d

Review the trans.log output — a clean run with no errors confirms successful connectivity between the ABAP application layer and HANA over SSL.

Summary

At this point, SSL encryption between the SAP ABAP application servers and SAP HANA is active using an externally signed CA certificate. The HANA server authenticates to the application layer via SAPSSLS.pse, while each ABAP node uses sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse as its trust store for verifying HANA's identity.

This guide was produced by the IT Planning and Software Logistics team, SAP Ireland, based on field experience from enterprise RISE migration projects.

entry.title: Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company or Pick your own SAP Best Practices. Which to choose?
entry.content:
Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company or Pick your own SAP Best Practices. Which to choose ?

Three acceleration options built on the same foundation — and how to pick the right one (or combine all three).

 

Figure 1 — Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices: three options built on SAP S/4HANA integrated processes, complementary and combinable.

One question. Three answers.

Every SAP S/4HANA transformation starts with the same decision: where do we begin?

Should you use:

  • Production Ready multinational preconfigured foundation that is built by SAP for your use case, addressing your Group, Tax & Localization requirements along with a setup which is tailored for you?
  • Leverage SAP's industry expertise through an executable reference solution that accelerates Fit-to-Standard and supports informed transformation decisions?
  • Or adopt proven standard business processes and configurations with the flexibility to select and activate the scope your organization needs?

Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices each answer this question differently. They are not competing products — they are all built on the same foundation — but they solve different problems, serve different customer profiles and come with very different delivery models.

Getting the choice wrong costs time. Getting it right — or knowing when to combine them — can take weeks off your Fit-to-Standard timeline before your first workshop even starts.

1. Enterprise Management Layer for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Production Ready Template for Multinational Organisations

For multinational organisations, the challenge in an S/4HANA transformation goes beyond validating standard processes. The system must support a consistent corporate operating model across different countries, legal entities, accounting principles and statutory obligations — all at once. This is a requirement even before Fit-to-standard workshops can begin.

Enterprise Management Layer is built for exactly that scenario. It delivers a preconfigured SAP S/4HANA multinational foundation, built by SAP for every customer, ready to deploy into your Development, Quality and Production landscape from the moment it is handed over. Business users can begin Fit-to-Standard validation on Day 1 once their Fit-to-Standard system is created — not after weeks of baseline setup.

The scope of what Enterprise Management Layer delivers out of the box is significant:

  • Up to 49 countries (43 SAP Best Practices countries + 6 Finance-led), localised and pre-activated
  • 25 system languages pre-installed, including Arabic, Chinese, Japanese and more
  • Three-ledger parallel accounting — Group GAAP, Local GAAP and Tax ledgers — configured and ready
  • Up to 220+ standard scope items active from Day 1
  • Additional Localisations for countries which are not yet available in Standard Best Practices.
  • Customer specific configuration such as 7 Service Options (VP01–VP07) covering intercompany, engineering, service processes and more — at no additional licence cost
  • Business process documentation, test scripts, configuration documents, how-to guides and process flow diagrams, all aligned to the delivered setup
  • Built by SAP to give you the peace of mind that the system will work as its designed by Experts for your individual needs.

Built by SAP, tailored to your configuration to enable your transformation decisions

Enterprise Management Layer is not a one-size-fits-all template. Every delivery starts with a customer questionnaire that captures the agreed configuration. The decisions made there directly shape the system SAP builds and delivers. Some of the details in the questionnaire are:

  • Country coverage — which countries and local requirements must be supported
  • Group currency — the currency for corporate reporting alongside local currencies
  • Fiscal-year variants — the corporate calendar and local reporting periods
  • Functional scope — standard scope, optional scope and Enterprise Management Layer -specific service options (for example, intercompany HQ and trading entity configurations)
  • Ledger design — a foundation for Group, Tax and Local GAAP reporting in a global setup

SAP builds the customer-specific image in the SAP staging area, delivers it as a database backup, and the system is usable on Day 1 after restoring from backup. The customer and project team then focus on Fit-to-Standard workshops and business validation — not on baseline setup.

Production Ready: What does it mean?

Customer and partner teams identify any additional requirements/changes specific to your organization —or “deltas”—between the delivered solution and the business requirements, determining what additional configuration or changes are needed. SAP-provided artefacts are compatible with the transformation toolchain, allowing these deltas to be reflected directly in updated Business Process Diagrams.

Once the agreed deltas have been configured and validated, the solution can progress towards production using the production-ready landscape established from the database copy provided by SAP.

For organisations seeking an even more tailored setup, SAP also offers an additional SAP Landscape Transformation service, for an extra charge, to adapt organisational structures to the customer's own nomenclature. The customer provides the required mapping, and SAP applies the corresponding changes to make the delivered setup more closely aligned with the customer's organisational structure. This is an optional, separately charged SAP service and is not included in Enterprise Management Layer.

More than pre-activated Best Practices

Enterprise Management Layer is built on SAP Best Practices, but it goes further. It adds multinational accounting design, enhanced country localisation, additional intercompany and supply-chain processes, Enterprise Management Layer-specific scope items and detailed implementation documentation — all pre-tested by SAP and patched before delivery. The project team inherits a foundation that SAP has already built and validated more than 400 times since 2012.

To know more about Enterprise Management Layer see my Blog and get in Fast Lane with Enterprise Management Layer 

For a thorough reading on Enterprise Management Layer, see blog Enterprise Management Layer Information Hub

Key differentiator: Enterprise Management Layer delivers a customer-specific multinational foundation — with depth in complex accounting, localisation, production-ready configuration and full implementation documentation — so the project team can start from substance, not from Scratch. That is: A working system for your setup, where your business users can see the processes working Live in Fit-to-Standard workshops. You can make decisions which matter for your business and fast forward your transformation. "Spend your time where it will matter the most with Enterprise Management Layer". 

2. Model Company: Industry expertise translated into an executable reference solution

SAP Best Practices establishes the standard process foundation for SAP S/4HANA. Model company for SAP cloud solutions takes this further by translating SAP's industry expertise and proven business practices into a preconfigured, executable industry reference solution. By bringing together integrated end-to-end business scenarios, industry-specific configuration, representative business data and transformation assets, it provides organisations with a tangible starting point for validating industry processes, accelerating Fit-to-Standard and making informed decisions about their future operating model.

From Fit-Gap habits to Fit-to-Standard decisions

A traditional Fit-Gap discussion often begins with a catalogue of existing processes and enhancements, then asks the new system to reproduce them. A stronger Fit-to-Standard approach begins with a proven reference process and asks a different question: can the business adopt this process, and if not, what is the justified business, regulatory or competitive reason for deviating?

Model Company supports that conversation through an integrated, executable industry reference, rather than only individual scope items or abstract diagrams. Participants can work through realistic end-to-end business scenarios, evaluate whether the proven process meets the business need, and justify deviations only where necessary. This turns Fit-to-Standard into an informed design discussion and supports clean-core decisions.

Industry expertise, executable content and the transformation toolchain

Model company's particular strength lies in translating industry knowledge into a working SAP environment. Depending on the industry, line-of-business offering and release, the available content can include:

  • Industry-specific, integrated end-to-end processes and scenarios configured in an executable reference environment.
  • Industry- and line-of-business-specific configuration with representative master and transactional data, where available.
  • Process models, flows, test scripts and supporting documentation reflecting the delivered reference content.
  • Relevant transformation artifacts for SAP Signavio, SAP LeanIX and SAP Cloud ALM, were published and subject to applicable tool access and content availability.
  • An industry-informed reference baseline that helps teams validate standard processes, assess necessary deviations and prepare implementation scope.

By connecting industry knowledge, business architecture, process design and executable scenarios, Model Company helps bridge the gap between conceptual transformation objectives and practical implementation decisions. The resulting emphasis on standardisation and clean-core principles also establishes a stronger foundation for evaluating future innovation and AI use cases.

Delivery and scope considerations

Model company for SAP cloud solutions is included under applicable RISE with SAP entitlements at no additional product charge, subject to the relevant terms and conditions. Depending on the offering, customers can access Model Company through pre-activated sandbox environments or self-service activation.

Industry-specific reference content is currently localised primarily for the United States and Germany, with the flexibility to extend configurations to up to three countries upon request, subject to additional service charges.

For customers requiring a combination of multiple industries and/or lines of business within a single environment, an assemble-to-order service is available. This allows compatible model company content to be brought together according to specific business requirements, subject to technical feasibility and additional service charges.

For broader multinational transformation requirements, model company and Enterprise Management Layer (EML) can also be combined to leverage their respective industry-specific and multinational capabilities. Such combinations require an assessment of scope, release compatibility and technical dependencies and may involve additional service charges.

Model company is intended as a reference and validation environment rather than a productive customer landscape.

For more information on Model Company, please read blog by Erik Rahm: Model Company for SAP Cloud Solutions

Key differentiator: Model Company translates SAP industry expertise into a configured, executable reference solution with connected scenarios and transformation content. Its value is in accelerating industry-informed Fit-to-Standard decisions, not simply assembling or demonstrating standard scope items.

3. SAP Best Practices for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Pick your own

SAP Best Practices are the standard, pre-built business process configurations — covering Finance, Procurement, Sales, Manufacturing, Supply Chain and more — that underpin every S/4HANA implementation. They represent the accumulated learning from thousands of SAP implementations and are available to every S/4HANA Private Cloud customer as part of the licence.

Crucially, SAP Best Practices are also the shared foundation on which both Enterprise Management Layer and Model Company are built. They are not a lesser option — they are the layer that makes all three approaches possible.

When an organization chooses to activate SAP Best Practices directly, without Enterprise Management Layer or model company, it benefits from the flexibility to select and activate standard business processes according to its implementation requirements. The project team determines the relevant scope and manages activation and configuration using SAP's standard tooling, taking into account applicable country coverage, release-specific availability and technical dependencies. Standard test scripts are available for 43 countries, providing additional guidance and support for process validation.

The trade-off is that the team takes on the associated technical groundwork: system preparation, process activation, post-activation configuration, testing and documentation. For organisations that want that level of control — particularly for single-country, lower-complexity implementations — this is entirely appropriate.

Key differentiator: SAP Best Practices provide proven standard business processes and configuration content, enabling implementation teams to select and activate relevant scope according to their business requirements, supported countries and technical dependencies. They establish a flexible foundation for adopting SAP standards and accelerating implementation.

4. How they compare

The table below captures the key differences across the dimensions that matter most in implementation decisions. Read across the columns to see which option fits your situation — or where combining them makes sense.

 Figure 2 — Detailed comparison: Enterprise Management Layer vs Model Company vs SAP Best Practices across ten capability dimensions.

5. Better together — the case for combining them

Consider a multinational automotive manufacturer seeking to harmonise financial processes across several countries while validating industry-specific production, sales and service scenarios with business stakeholders:

  • Enterprise Management Layer (EML) provides a preconfigured multinational foundation, including organisational structures, accounting frameworks, ledger configurations, extensive country localisation and customer specific configurations build by SAP. This reduces initial configuration effort and establishes a validated baseline for multinational implementation.
  • Model company for SAP cloud solutions translates SAP's industry expertise into a preconfigured, executable industry reference solution. With integrated end-to-end business scenarios, industry-specific configuration, representative business data and supporting transformation assets, it enables stakeholders to experience proven industry practices and accelerate Fit-to-Standard validation.
  • SAP Best Practices provides the underlying standard business processes and configurations, offering flexibility to evaluate and activate additional relevant scope according to the customer's business requirements and implementation strategy.

Together, these offerings can provide a comprehensive transformation starting point, combining multinational capabilities, executable industry-specific processes and established SAP standards. By leveraging preconfigured and validated content, organisations can reduce initial setup effort, accelerate business validation and make more informed design decisions while supporting a clean-core approach.

Practical consideration: Combining these offerings requires an assessment of release compatibility, configuration dependencies, functional scope and delivery requirements. The feasibility and effort involved depend on the selected content and customer-specific circumstances; combined scenarios are not automatically validated end-to-end.

6. Which one is right for your project?

Use the profiles below as a starting guide. Most large programmes will find themselves drawn to more than one — which is exactly the point.

If your situation is…

Start with…

Complex Multinational Operations requiring parallel accounting, multi country localisation and tailored configurations – build for every Customer by SAP giving a solid production ready foundation.

Enterprise Management Layer — SAP built customer tailored foundation, prepared and tested for your requirements. Accelerate Fit-to-standard with clean core starting point and a production ready path forward.

Industry-specific exploration and early-phase validation — business stakeholders need to see realistic, connected scenarios before committing to process design

Model Company — Delivers an executable, industry-specific reference solution that accelerates Fit-to-Standard. Included under applicable RISE with SAP entitlements. For multinational transformations, Model Company and Enterprise Management Layer can be combined to leverage their respective strengths.

Standard, lower-complexity S/4HANA implementation — full control over scope selection, single-country or simple multi-country, team handles activation

SAP Best Practices — select your scope, activate with SAP tooling, build at your own pace. Available in 43 countries, included with the S/4HANA licence.

7. The goal is not to choose a winner

Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices are not competing answers to the same question. Each solves a different problem.

Enterprise Management Layer accelerates transformation of a multinational by delivering preconfigured financial ledgers & localization for 49 countries with additional customer specific configurations such as Intercompany setup between Headquarter & Trading Company. This provides a solid fast forward start to fit-to-standard and a foundation which can be taken to production by just configuring delta (any additional requirements or changes specific to your organization you identify) on top.

Model company for SAP cloud solutions translates SAP's industry expertise into a preconfigured, executable reference solution, enabling business stakeholders, architects and implementation teams to validate proven industry processes, accelerate Fit-to-Standard and make informed design decisions based on a tangible, working baseline.

SAP Best Practices provide implementation teams with a proven foundation of standard business processes and configurations, offering the flexibility to select and activate the scope that best aligns with their business requirements and implementation strategy.

Used together, Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company for SAP cloud solutions and SAP Best Practices bring together complementary strengths in multinational capabilities, industry-specific expertise and standard business processes. This provides a comprehensive, preconfigured foundation that accelerates transformation, reduces implementation effort and supports a consistent Fit-to-Standard approach.

The real question is not which solution to choose, but how to leverage their respective strengths, individually or together, to accelerate transformation, embrace proven industry practices and establish a sustainable foundation for future innovation.

entry.title: Model company for SAP cloud solutions for Architects: From Target Architecture to an Executable Base
entry.content:
Part 2 of a blog series on model company for SAP cloud solutions

Introduction

 

Every architect knows the moment: the target architecture is documented in capability maps, process models and solution designs, but the next question is how to turn that intent into decisions the implementation team can validate and deliver.

This is my second post in the model company for SAP cloud solutions series. The first post introduced the overall proposition and the move toward Fit-to-Standard. Here, the focus is on the decisions enterprise and solution architects need to make.

Model company provides a pre-configured, executable SAP S/4HANA reference baseline with available industry and line-of-business content. It does not define every customer’s target architecture. Instead, it gives architects a working reference against which to assess capability coverage, question assumptions and identify the design decisions that remain.

Figure 1: From architectural intent to an executable reference. Model company provides a baseline for validation, not a finished customer architecture.

The Architect’s Challenge: From Design to Executable Reality

 

Target architectures describe what an organization wants to achieve; implementation teams must determine how that intent can be realized in a configured solution. The handover between the two often exposes uncertainties: Is a process already supported by standard SAP functionality? Which assumptions need testing? What requires integration, configuration or an extension?

Model company helps bridge this gap by making relevant standard processes and industry content tangible. Architects can explore and demonstrate a working reference rather than relying exclusively on diagrams or descriptions. The reference does not remove the need for discovery or customer-specific validation; it makes those activities more focused.

This supports a change in mindset, from Fit-to-Gap (“how do we reproduce what we do today?”) to Fit-to-Standard (“can the standard support the intended outcome, and where is differentiation genuinely necessary?”). The question is not whether the standard is always sufficient, but how to make deviations evidence-based architectural decisions.

Figure 2: Changing the conversation: assess business outcomes against the standard before specifying deviations.

An Architect’s Workflow: A Retail Example

 

Consider an illustrative retail transformation. The target architecture calls for improved inventory visibility, a consistent order-fulfillment process and reliable financial integration. Rather than treating every existing customization as a requirement, the architecture team can use the relevant model company reference to structure its assessment.

  • Identify the capabilities: map the target business outcomes to the processes and application responsibilities that must support them.
  • Explore the baseline: examine available retail processes and associated artifacts in the model company system. Confirm which scope and release are available.
  • Validate assumptions: demonstrate representative flows with sample data; compare the standard with key business scenarios and record the functional or non-functional questions still open.
  • Make design choices: Distinguish standard coverage from required configuration, interfaces, data work, and genuinely differentiating extensions. For each proposed deviation, document its justification, expected business value, and implications for complexity, cost, and long-term maintainability.
  • Carry decisions into delivery: use relevant process models, scope artifacts and governance tools to connect decisions to implementation requirements, testing and change control.

The result is not an automatically generated target architecture. It is a better-evidenced design: the team knows what it has validated, where uncertainty remains and which decisions require architectural ownership.

 

How It Helps Enterprise Architects

 

Enterprise architects connect strategy, business capabilities and the target operating model with the application landscape.

Model company can help them:

  • Assess capability realization in a running reference and distinguish demonstrated scope from capabilities that still require further design.
  • Relate reference business architecture and process models to the actual standard processes delivered in the relevant industry or line of business.
  • Create a shared starting point for business stakeholders, enterprise architecture and delivery teams, reducing misunderstandings about what “standard” means.
  • Inform roadmap and scoping decisions by checking current content availability, release coverage and relevant prerequisites rather than assuming that every planned capability is already delivered.

How It Helps Solution Architects

 

Solution architects translate the target into process, data, application, integration and extension decisions. Against a pre-configured reference, they can:

  • Explore representative end-to-end processes instead of starting each discussion from an unconfigured system.
  • Inspect sample master and transactional data and identify interfaces or integration requirements; a visible integration point does not necessarily mean that a connected external system has been delivered.
  • Evaluate standard functionality first, then select suitable clean-core-aligned extensibility options based on the requirement and deployment environment.
  • Use process and delivery artifacts to support documented scope, requirements and testing decisions, with traceability governed through the chosen project toolchain.

Connecting Architecture to the Delivery Toolchain

 

SAP LeanIX supports enterprise architecture and application landscape decisions; SAP Signavio provides a comprehensive process intelligence and transformation suite for process-modeling and business transformation; and SAP Cloud ALM is a full lifecycle application management platform, covering implementation governance, operations monitoring, and continuous improvement.

For transformation initiatives, it delivers end-to-end project management, structured requirements handling, and test governance, making it the central control point for managing SAP solution deployments.

Model company contributes a working reference and associated artifacts that can be used alongside these tools.

The precise artifacts available depend on the selected model company scope and release. Process models, documentation, test assets and sample data can support design and Fit-to-Standard workshops, but architects should verify what is included and how it can be accessed or imported. Viewing process content and importing or synchronizing it into a customer workspace may have different licensing and authorization requirements.

Importantly, traceability is not automatic. Connecting process models, scope, requirements and test evidence requires tool configuration, appropriate entitlements, disciplined ownership and project governance. SAP Signavio, SAP Cloud ALM synchronization, for example, has defined setup and license prerequisites.

 

Where It Fits in SAP Activate

 

Model company brings its most immediate value to early validation and Fit-to-Standard work, particularly during Explore. Its reference content and artifacts may also inform later implementation phases.

The model company system remains a reference/sandbox environment: it is not the productive customer solution and should not be described as directly deploying into production.

  • Discover and Prepare: use the available baseline to illustrate potential scope, challenge target-state assumptions and prepare more focused architectural discussions.
  • Explore (Fit-to-Standard): run relevant scenarios against the standard, assess business fit, identify genuine deltas and agree which requirements need additional design.
  • Realize: use validated decisions and applicable reference artifacts to guide implementation; govern architecture conformance, interfaces, extensions and test coverage in the customer project.
  • Deploy: confirm that the implemented productive solution meets the approved architecture, security, integration and operational criteria. This is a customer-project responsibility, not a deployment of the model company sandbox.
  • Run: maintain architectural guardrails, assess changing needs against standard capabilities, and govern extensions and process evolution over time.

The continuous thread is controlled decision-making: from intended business capability, through process validation and design, to implementation evidence. The architecture team can establish traceability across that chain but must actively maintain it.

Figure 3: Model company in SAP Activate. Explore is the primary direct validation point; later phases benefit from the reference and decisions carried forward.

Keeping the Core Clean: Extensibility Governance

 

Clean core is an architectural discipline, not a property that eliminates governance. It aims to keep the SAP core close to standard, use appropriate extension mechanisms and released interfaces, and support maintainability and future upgrades. Model company, built on SAP Best Practices that bring standard Line of Business business processes and aligned with clean-core principles, gives architects a useful starting reference, not an unconditional guarantee of customer-specific compliance or upgrade safety.

  • Challenge proposed deviations: demonstrate what standard content already covers before agreeing to custom build; record business rationale and architectural consequences for justified gaps.
  • Choose the right extension pattern: consider approved key-user, developer/on-stack and side-by-side extensibility, including SAP BTP where appropriate. The right choice depends on requirements, release and deployment model; “side-by-side” is not the answer to every extension.
  • Govern integration explicitly: design interfaces around applicable released APIs and supported integration patterns, while validating external systems, security, performance and data responsibilities.
  • Keep decisions traceable: link requirements, architectural decisions, process changes and tests within the project’s governed toolchain, rather than assuming the reference environment does this automatically.

By reducing unnecessary custom code and providing a clean-core-aligned reference, model company simplifies architectural decision-making and lifecycle management, while enabling architects to focus their assessments on customer-specific requirements, integrations, and extensions.

 

What Architects Still Need to Validate

 

A reference baseline is most useful when its boundaries are clear.

Architects must still confirm:

  • Industry and country coverage
  • Business-process fit
  • The customer’s application and integration landscape
  • Data migration and ownership
  • Non-functional requirements
  • Security and regulatory obligations
  • Extension design
  • Licensing or technical prerequisites for connected tools.

The strongest use of model company is therefore not to declare the architecture complete. It is to expose and resolve architectural questions earlier, while keeping legitimate differentiation visible and controlled.

 

From Clean Core to Validated AI Capabilities

 

Clean-core principles, standardized processes, and governed data provide a strong foundation for sustainable AI adoption. Model company for SAP cloud solutions builds on this foundation, with Joule already activated and successfully tested in selected model company environments. In addition, AI use cases have been tested and validated and are ready for inclusion, progressively extending the portfolio’s ability to demonstrate AI-enabled business processes.

For architects, this creates an opportunity to move beyond conceptual AI discussions and explore how intelligent capabilities can be incorporated into business processes and solution architectures. These validated scenarios provide tangible reference points for assessing architectural dependencies, integration requirements, and the potential role of AI within a customer’s target landscape.

AI enablement is progressing across the model company portfolio, with capabilities and availability varying by industry and line of business. Their adoption within a customer environment remains subject to scenario availability, release compatibility, licensing and entitlements, technical prerequisites, and applicable AI consumption arrangements.

By combining a clean-core-aligned baseline with activated Joule capabilities and validated AI use cases, model company helps architects bridge the gap between AI strategy and practical enablement.

 

Conclusion: A Better Starting Point for Architectural Decisions

 

Model company changes the starting point, not the architect’s responsibility. Instead of working only from abstract models or a blank configuration, teams can examine a tangible, SAP-delivered baseline and use it to validate assumptions, challenge unnecessary complexity and make more informed Fit-to-Standard decisions.

Whether your role is enterprise architecture or solution architecture, the benefit is a clearer distinction between what the reference already demonstrates, what the customer genuinely needs and what must still be designed and governed.

Start with one critical capability from your target architecture. Explore the model company content available for the relevant industry, test the associated process assumptions and document where the standard fits or where further decisions are needed.

What is the harder challenge in your projects:

  • Validating standard coverage
  • Designing integrations
  • Governing extensions?
